bio.en: Tom Conrad is the CEO of Zero and a veteran product and technology leader who helped build foundational iOS features at Apple, served as CTO of Pandora and VP of Product at Snap, and was an executive at the famed failures Pets.com and Quibi.
bio.zh: Tom Conrad 是 Zero 的 CEO，也是一位资深的产品与技术领导者：他曾在 Apple 帮助打造 iOS 的基础性功能，担任过 Pandora 的 CTO 与 Snap 的产品副总裁，还曾任职于那些著名的失败案例 Pets.com 与 Quibi。

summary.en: Tom reflects on lessons from both billion-dollar failures (Pets.com, Quibi) and billion-dollar successes (Apple, Pandora, Snap), including why not everyone needs to be a founder. He shares how to choose where to work, the math of a business, and how to avoid burnout while building. The episode is a rare, story-rich blend of failure and success from a true operator.
summary.zh: Tom 反思了十亿美元级失败（Pets.com、Quibi）与十亿美元级成功（Apple、Pandora、Snap）中的经验，包括为什么并非人人都需要成为创始人。他分享了如何选择供职的公司、生意背后的数学逻辑，以及如何在打造产品的同时避免职业倦怠。本期是一位真正从业者对失败与成功的、富含故事的罕见融合。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: There's this belief that everybody needs to be a founder. I think, in some ways, our industry would be much better off if there were fewer founders. There's an entire category of smart, creative, hardworking, talented, borderline visionary people who can raise that $2 million seed and go off and build some stupid company that's never going to go anywhere. That would be so much better off finding a team that needs their skillset and working on a problem that has a mathematical formula that's going to win on any metric. Whatever metric you care about. You want the acclaim of your peers, you want financial reward, you want outside impact on culture, whatever the thing is that gets you out of bed every morning, you can achieve that in collaboration with others. You don't have to be the person that raises the seed round.
turns.zh: 有人认为每个人都必须成为创业者。但在我看来，如果创业者数量减少，我们这个行业或许会更好。在这个行业里，有太多聪明、富有创造力、勤奋且才华横溢的人——甚至近乎有远见卓识的人——他们能筹到200万美元种子资金，却创办一些注定难成大业的愚蠢公司。这些人才若能加入需要他们技能的团队，专注于解决存在数学公式、能在任何指标上胜出的难题，无论是渴望同行认可、追求经济回报，还是致力于对文化产生深远影响——只要能激发你每天早晨起床的动力——都能在与他人合作中实现目标。没必要非得亲自去筹集种子轮资金。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I thought it'd be fun to start with a story about your time at Apple and you building this now very ubiquitous feature of dragging and dropping something into a folder. Which I saw you tweet about or talk about at a talk and the fact that it's still around. Can you just share that story and maybe a lesson from that experience that you've taken away?
turns.zh: 我想先从你在苹果公司的经历讲起，当时你开发了一个现在已被广泛应用的功能——将某个元素拖放到文件夹中。记得你曾在推特上分享过这个故事，还在某次演讲中提及过它，而这个功能至今仍在使用。你能否分享一下这个故事，以及从中获得的经验教训？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: Sure. Let's see. I was 15 years old when the Macintosh came out. I remember really clearly my entire teenage years. All I wanted to do was to move from Columbus, Ohio to Cupertino and work for Apple. My heroes were that team of people that had written their signatures on the inside of the Macintosh. We cracked open the first Macintosh case. You would find the signatures of the 20 people or so who worked on the Mac. That was my only ambition, truly. (00:05:40): This was a period where no one wanted to work for Apple. That wasn't a thing. It seems like maybe a little obvious today, but it wasn't an obvious ambition at all back then. Anyway, I went to college. It's all I wanted to do. Studied computer engineering at University of Michigan, and as we talk about my career, it is just over and over and over. I'm going to say an incredibly lucky thing happened. The first incredibly lucky thing that happened for me in my career probably was that University of Michigan happened to be a place that Apple recruited from. (00:06:08): I didn't know that when I chose the school, but it made it reasonably easy to connect to a hiring manager at Apple. I wrote an actual letter and put it in an actual envelope and put it in the mail and got an internship and drove out in my dad's Pontiac from the Midwest to California. Spent a summer interning and my last day of the internship, I was thinking about really what I wanted to do when I came back. Hopefully came back to Apple after I graduated. (00:06:39): I had worked on a product that became shipped. It was called the QuickDraw GX. It was earlier second generation rendering system for the Mac. I'd been that team's intern for the summer. But what I really wanted to do is I wanted to work on the Finder. This is the only thing in the whole world I really wanted to do. I went and found Ron Lichty, who is the manager of the Finder team and said, "I graduate in 10 months. I'd love to be a part of your team." (00:07:06): I think he was like, why are you coming and talking to me now? You're literally going back to Michigan tomorrow. I go back to Michigan in May, the phone rings and Ron says, "The college recruiting department just told me that I have a college hiring rep and if I don't use it by tomorrow, I lose it." He's like, "I can't even interview you, you can't meet the team, but you're basically a freebie for me. Do you want this job?" (00:07:38): Just insanely lucky moment, got this job. I get to Apple in the summer of 1992 and I have a laundry list of things that I would like to do to make the Finder more usable. I remember sitting in Ron's office and saying, "At the grocery store, when you're carrying bags of groceries out, the door's automatically open for you? I think the Finder should do the same thing. When you're dragging an icon around and you want to put it in a folder, you should be able to hover maybe over the folder icons and drill down into the file system to get to where you're going. (00:08:20): Then when you drop the file, all of the folders that opened up between you and your source and your destination would close for you." Ron thought that was a fine idea, so that was the way Apple worked in those days. I just went off and started coding that up. I got to the point late one night, two in the morning at Apple, no one else was there, where I needed some kind of animation to indicate that the folder was about to open. (00:08:48): I'm certainly not an animator and I certainly wasn't going to do anything thoughtful in the middle of the night. I just wrote some code that blinked the folder, like selected unselected, selected unselected five times and thought, oh, I'll email one of the really talented visual designers to do something much more interesting. Long story short, apple finally shipped that feature four years later. Sat in the source code repository forever while we did other things. (00:09:21): When it shipped four years later, it blinked five times. Roll the clock forward six or seven years, Mac plus 10 comes out, entirely new Finder rewritten from scratch. No spring-loaded folders anywhere to be seen. People complained about it. It got re-implemented. All of the code, brand new. Folder blinks five times when you hover over it. Roll the clock forward another decade, IOS comes along and they added folders. When you drag an icon around, it blinks a few times. (00:09:51): I'm not sure what the point of this story is other than maybe it's something about, I think we all do this as designers and product people. We take these shortcuts that we think that we'll go back later and clean up. Sometimes, it's literally been 30 years that little design detail lingers three implementations later and now it's just a part of the way that these Apple products work. Pretty bizarre.
turns.zh:
好的。让我想想。我15岁那年，Macintosh刚问世。我清楚地记得整个青少年时期的经历。我当时唯一的愿望就是从俄亥俄州的哥伦布市搬到加利福尼亚州的库比蒂诺，为苹果公司工作。那些在Macintosh内部签下署名的团队成员至今仍令我心驰神往。我们拆开Macintosh的外壳时，会发现里面有20位左右参与开发人员的签名。这确实是我唯一的梦想。（00:05:40）：那时根本没人想去苹果工作。那不是一个热门选择。如今看来或许显而易见，但在当时这绝对算不上一个显而易见的抱负。总之，我上了大学。这是我唯一想做的事。我在密歇根大学学习计算机工程，回顾我的职业生涯，似乎这条道路始终在不断重叠。我要说，我遇到了极其幸运的机遇。职业生涯中最幸运的转折之一，或许就是密歇根大学恰好是苹果公司的招聘目标学校。（00:06:08）：我选择这所学校时并不知道这一点，但这让我能相对轻松地联系到苹果公司的招聘经理。我亲手写了一封信，装进信封寄出去，最终获得了实习机会。于是我开着父亲的庞蒂克汽车，从中西部驱车前往加州。实习结束那天，我思考着回校后该何去何从。希望毕业后能重返苹果。（00:06:39）：我参与过一款最终投入市场的产品——QuickDraw GX，这是Macintosh的第二代渲染系统。我那年夏天在该团队实习。但我真正想做的是参与Finder的开发。这是我唯一想做的事。我找到Finder团队经理Ron Lichty，说：“我还有10个月就毕业了。我很想加入你们的团队。”（00:07:06）：他当时大概在想：“你现在来找我干什么？明天你就要回密歇根了。”5月份我回到密歇根，电话铃响起，Ron说：“招聘部门通知我，有个校园招聘名额，如果不及时用掉就作废了。” 他说：“我甚至没法面试你，也没法让团队见你，但你可以免费加入。想不想来？”（00:07:38）：真是天助我也，我得到了这份工作。1992年夏天加入苹果后，我列了一长串提升Finder易用性的想法。我记得在Ron的办公室里说：“去超市时，手提袋自动打开？Finder也应该这样。当你拖动图标到文件夹时，能否悬停在文件夹图标上，并深入文件系统查找目标文件？”（00:08:20）：然后当你放下文件时，所有打开的文件夹都会自动关闭。Ron觉得这个主意不错，这就是当时苹果的开发模式。我随即开始编写代码。深夜两点钟，苹果园区空无一人，当时我需要用某种动画效果来显示文件夹即将打开的状态。（00:08:48）：我绝不是动画师，也不可能在深夜做出精心设计。我只是写了段让文件夹闪烁的代码。
比如，选中、未选中，选中、未选中操作重复了五次，然后我心想，哦，我应该给某位才华横溢的视觉设计师发邮件，让他们设计出更有趣的东西。长话短说，四年后苹果终于上线了那个功能。它在源代码库里躺了好久，我们忙着做其他事情。（00:09:21）四年后正式发布时，那个功能只闪烁了五下。再往前推六七年，Mac Plus 10发布，Finder彻底重写，完全没有弹簧式文件夹的影子。用户抱怨不已，后来又重新实现了这个功能，所有代码都是全新的。当鼠标悬停在文件夹上时，文件夹还是会闪烁五下。再往后推十年，iOS出现了，他们又添加了文件夹功能。当你拖动图标时，文件夹会闪烁几下。（00:09:51）我不确定这个故事的重点是什么，或许只是想说，作为设计师和产品经理，我们都曾这样做过。当时为了省事，觉得以后会回头修改。但有时候，这个小小的设计细节会在三个版本后依然存在，最终成为苹果产品运行机制的一部分。真是不可思议。

Over your career, you've landed at a lot of really successful places. You've also landed at a lot of very famous failures that we're going to talk about. What advice would you give people for helping them pick where to go work based on your experience?
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，我想谈谈如何选择工作地点的问题。显然你很想去苹果工作。回顾你的职业生涯，你去过很多非常成功的地方，也经历过很多失败的项目。我们接下来要讨论这些失败的项目。基于你的经验，你会给人们什么建议，帮助他们选择合适的工作地点？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: When I was a kid, my ambition to work at Apple was entirely about the product, so probably that version of me would say, find a product that you're passionate about and go spend your time and energy on that thing. Pretty quickly you learn that an awful lot of your development and day-to-day satisfaction really comes from the people that you get to collaborate with. Can you learn from them? Do you like them? Do they challenge you in the right ways? (00:11:53): Do they give you latitude in the right ways? It's so much about not just what, but who. For a very long time, my advice would've been entirely in the category of life, find something that you love with people that you think are amazing and the rest will take care of itself. Interestingly, I have been lucky enough to have some things that were successful on the metrics, get talked about the most, big audiences, big financial return, et cetera, et cetera. I've also worked on some things that were really notable disasters. When I look back on my career and think about the things that I've done, my professional satisfaction is not well correlated with those external metrics and very, very coordinated with do I love the thing we were building and do I love the people I was working with?
turns.zh: 我小时候想在苹果工作完全是因为产品，所以那个时候的我可能会说，找一个你热爱的产品，然后投入时间和精力去做它。很快你就会发现，开发过程和日常满足感很大程度上来自于合作伙伴。你能从他们身上学习吗？你喜欢他们吗？他们能以正确的方式挑战你吗？（00:11:53）他们能以正确的方式给你足够的自由吗？这不仅关乎产品本身，还关乎团队成员。很长一段时间以来，我的建议完全基于生活层面：找到你热爱的事业，找到你认为很棒的人，其他的自然而然就会到位。很有趣的是，我很幸运地有一些在指标上成功的产品，获得了最多的关注，吸引了大量观众，带来了丰厚的经济回报等等。但我也参与过一些非常显著的失败项目。当我回顾自己的职业生涯，思考我做过的事情时，我的职业满足感与这些外部指标并不高度相关，而与我是否热爱我们正在开发的产品，以及我是否喜欢一起工作的团队高度相关。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Following the thread of the people. I think one of the hardest things is really knowing what the people are like until you join. I think as a chief product officer joining or VP of product, you have a lot of time that you spend with the team. Most people don't. They have an interview and then they're like, all right, I got to make a decision. Do you have any advice for how to help people get a sense if the people are the kind of people they want to work with?
turns.zh: 顺着团队的思路。我认为最难的事情之一就是在加入团队之前真正了解团队成员是什么样的。作为首席产品官或产品副总裁加入团队时，你会花很多时间与团队在一起。但大多数人不会这样。他们参加面试，然后就得做决定。你有什么建议能帮助人们判断团队成员是否是他们想一起工作的人吗？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: I think people are really, really good at this. Every single time I've taken a job where it turned out that I was working with people who had a different set of values or working styles than I had, I knew. You tell yourself that, at least in my case, I tell myself a story about why the thing I suspect might be the case isn't the case. But you do this in your personal life all the time. You meet people out at dinner, so you get seated next to them at some industry event or something, and sometimes you come home and say to your partner, oh my gosh, the person next to me was just the worst. Then sometimes you're like, I think I made a permanent lifelong connection with this total stranger who just happened to sit next to me.
turns.zh: 我觉得人们在这方面真的、真的很擅长。每次我接到一份工作，结果发现同事们的价值观或工作方式与我截然不同时，我都能察觉到这一点。你会告诉自己——至少我自己是这样——编造各种理由来否定自己的怀疑。但这种情况在个人生活中也屡见不鲜。比如参加行业活动时坐在某人旁边，共进晚餐时与某人同桌，回家后你可能会对伴侣说"天哪，旁边那个人简直糟透了"；或者相反地感叹"我觉得我和这位偶然坐在我旁边的陌生人结下了终身难忘的缘分"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a very simple piece of advice that I think people don't fully appreciate is just trust your instinct, trust your gut. Just pay attention to what comes up when you're around people at a certain company. Okay, you brought up this phrase of notable disasters, and I want to talk about that. You've worked at two of the most famous notable disasters of product companies, pets.com and Quibi. I think it's really rare someone sees the inside of so much hype and then such a fall at a company. I just want to spend some time in these two areas. Maybe the way to set it up is, what's a lesson you took away from each of these two experiences that you've taken with you to future work and maybe advice you share with people?
turns.zh: 有一条非常简单的建议，我觉得人们没有充分领会，那就是要相信自己的直觉。只要留意与某家公司同事相处时产生的种种感受。比如你提到的两大知名产品公司——Pets.com和Quibi，它们都曾是轰动一时的成功案例，最终却以失败告终。我觉得能亲身见证一家公司从万众瞩目到一败涂地的人实在少之又少。接下来我想重点探讨这两个案例。或许可以这样展开：你从这两次经历中分别获得了哪些教训，又将这些经验带入了后续的工作中？或许你还能给其他人一些建议？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: Probably the biggest lesson, it's not really about the specifics of the business. The biggest lesson really is these things make you better. In some instances, actually, I think in both instances they became dominoes that opened doors for me in my own ambition and my own professional life that maybe just wouldn't have opened at all if I hadn't gone to those companies and learned those things and had those experiences. Frankly, even in the case of pets.com, even the high profile nature of it. (00:15:09): I could have worked at one of a thousand E-commerce websites in 1999. When I went on to some subsequent job interview or something and talked about my experience, they were like, I never heard of the thing that you worked on. But everybody certainly heard about pets.com. It's a pretty funny example too, of how some struggles are timeless. That was 23, 24 years ago now. While as a leadership team, we made I'm sure all kinds of mistakes. (00:15:39): One of the things that happened was that there were three overfunded pet E-commerce sites. We all raised in excess of $50 million, which is a tremendous amount of money now. It was a tremendous amount of money then. We all thought it was a zero-sum game. That as one player started to spend on promotion or to spend irrationally on national broadcast television advertising, we all did. It became this unwinnable arms race. There is, I think, a fundamental lesson about having an excess of investment can be its own albatross. Or lead you to make decisions that maybe would be unwise. Then of course, it's just like timing is really important. Chewy is a online pet store worth $9 billion today. They were a private company and bought by PetSmart and then spun back out. But when they were bought by PetSmart, they were acquired for three billion dollars. Biggest E-commerce acquisition of all time. Well, I think it's probably unfair to compare Chewy who executed exceptionally well over a decade, grew their business brick by brick and turned it into something really remarkable. (00:17:07): To pets.com, which was in a very, very different moment in time and tried to go to market in a really different way. The critique that is often leveled at pets.com, or at least at the time, was like, this is just a stupid business. They're shipping dog food around. You could never make that work. That's just wrong. You absolutely can make it work. Probably can't make it work when 80% of the country on the internet is still on dial up. It was really, really early.
turns.zh: 或许最重要的教训并非具体的商业细节。真正重要的在于，这些经历能让你不断成长。在某些情况下，我认为这两段经历就像多米诺骨牌，为我自己的事业抱负和职业生涯打开了新的大门。如果我没有加入那些公司、学习那些技能、积累那些经验，这些机会或许根本不会降临。说实话，即便是在pets.com的案例中，尽管它备受瞩目，但1999年我本可以选择千千万万家电商网站中的任何一家。后来参加面试时，当我谈起自己的经历时，对方往往会说"从没听说过你做过的那个项目"。但pets.com却家喻户晓。这也是一个有趣的例子，说明有些挫折是永恒的。那是23、24年前的事了。作为领导团队，我们肯定犯过各种错误。（00:15:09）：其中一个教训是，当时有三个过度融资的宠物电商网站。我们各自融资超过5000万美元，在当时这是一笔巨额资金。当时我们都认为这是一场零和博弈——当一家公司开始在推广上投入过多资金，或不理性地投放全国性电视广告时，其他公司也会效仿。这就形成了无法取胜的军备竞赛。我认为过度投资可能成为自己的累赘，或导致做出不明智的决策。当然，时机也至关重要。如今Chewy是一家价值90亿美元的在线宠物商店。他们曾是私营公司，被PetSmart收购后又被分拆上市。但被PetSmart收购时，Chewy的估值高达30亿美元，创下电商收购史上最高纪录。不过我觉得将Chewy与pets.com比较并不公平。Chewy在过去十年间执行得极为出色，业务稳步增长，最终成为行业标杆。而pets.com则处于截然不同的时代背景下，尝试以完全不同的方式进入市场。人们对pets.com的批评（至少在当时）是"这就是个愚蠢的商业模式"、"他们只会送货上门"、"这根本行不通"。这些观点大错特错。只要80%的网民仍在使用拨号上网，成功几乎无从谈起。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I saw a stat, I think you shared somewhere, that you took pets.com from nothing to a public company to completely out of business in 19 months.
turns.zh: 我记得你曾分享过一项数据：你们在19个月内就将pets.com从无到有，发展为上市公司，最终又走向倒闭。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's about right. The other thing that's forgotten in the tale is that we actually didn't go bankrupt. We shut the company down and returned the remaining balance to the investors, which no public company had ever done before. The leadership team just reached the conclusion that given the way market conditions had evolved, there was just no way we were going to be able to get more capital into the company. It was a company that required additional investment to get to profitability. It was better to wind down early, take the money that we had in the bank and get it back to investors than to just spend every last penny on what was a fruitless attempt to salvage it.
turns.zh: 是的，情况大致如此。但这个故事中被忽略的一点是，我们实际上并未破产。我们关闭了公司，将剩余资金返还给投资者，这是史无前例的举动。领导团队得出结论：鉴于市场环境的变化，我们根本无法为公司筹集更多资金。这是一家需要额外投资才能实现盈利的公司。与其耗尽最后一分钱试图挽救它，不如尽早结束业务，将银行存款返还给投资者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did not know that. Let's talk about Quibi. What went wrong there? Do you think there was a path to Quibi having worked out? Any big lessons that you took away from that experience that you bring with you?
turns.zh: 真不知道这回事。那咱们来聊聊Quibi吧。Quibi到底是哪儿出了问题？你觉得Quibi原本有可能成功吗？从这次经历中你有什么重要的启发可以分享吗？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: The miraculous thing about Quibi for me was it re-lit my enthusiasm for the industry for doing this work. I had left in, I think it was December of 2018, and I thought that maybe I was just done making software. I had done it for a really long time, for 25 years or something. I had changed a lot. The industry had changed a lot. I thought maybe I just didn't have the same passion for it that I had a decade before. It also seemed like maybe it'd be fun to have another chapter of my life that was just completely different. (00:19:23): I had a whole list of things that I thought I might want to do. They're ridiculous. It's like maybe I want to be a pastry chef. Maybe I want to be a landscape photographer. Maybe I want to learn to make bad music to put up on SoundCloud or something. Really the only thing they had in common were they all things that I knew nothing about. People would be like, "Oh, you think you might want to be a pastry chef? Do you like to bake?" (00:19:42): I'd be like, "No, I don't know anything about baking." "Oh, you like landscape photography. Do you take photos?" "No, I don't take photos." But I was committed to the bit, actually to the point where when Techwrench interviewed me about my departure from Snapchat, I was like, I'm out. I'm going to do something else entirely. That story is very much out there. But a few months after my last day at Snap, I got a call from Meg Whitman and Jeffrey Katzenberg who were starting up, it was for New TV at the time. (00:20:15): The pitch was, we're going to try to take the best of mobile and Silicon Valley and consumer tech and weld it to the best of Hollywood style content production. To build something completely bespoke and purpose made for consumption on the phone. They were looking for both technology leadership and product leadership and wanted to know if I was interested in one or both. I took the meeting, even though I wasn't really taking these kinds of calls from anybody, it just seemed like who's going to pass up the opportunity to have lunch with the two of them? (00:20:50): I listened to the pitch and politely declined and told them that I was going to be a pastry chef or something. We kept doing that every couple of months for seven months. We'd go to lunch, they would give me an update on the progress they were making, and I would decline the invitation to get involved somehow. Then late in that year, I went to lunch one more time, and Meg explained that they brought on someone to lead technology and they brought another person to lead product. (00:21:26): Both of them really truly for reasons that are completely disconnected from Quibi itself. Both of them had left after about six weeks. Meg's like, "We've raised all this money and we told the world that we're shipping this product in about a year. We got an awful lot to do, and I really could use some help. I would consider it a personal favor if you were to come and spend just a couple of days a week helping." She's like, "I'll continue to look for someone who actually wants the job, but it'd be great if you could help me get this off the ground." My wife is a freelance writer, marketing strategist, and loves her life as a freelance contributor. She's like, "You should do this. Why not? It's two days a week. It's just a few months. What's the worst thing that could happen? Maybe you'll like it?" I'm like, "No. Here's the thing that will happen. I won't do it two days a week. It will immediately be three days, then four days, then five days, then six days. I just know myself." (00:22:27): She's like, "No." She's like, "Just on Wednesday night at six o'clock, close your Quibi laptop and be like, all they're paying me for is for Tuesday and Wednesday and then open it back up on Tuesday morning. That's all you've got to do." Well, she's right about most things and she's wrong about this. I fell deeply into it right away. It was just so fun to get to build a team from scratch and to design and build a product from scratch. (00:22:58): To take advantage of all of the modern software architecture stuff that had come into being over the course of the 15 years since we had started Pandora. I'm embarrassed about some of what happened with Quibi for sure, but I'm super grateful for the experience. I just really fell in love with the industry again, and was reminded of just how rewarding it can be to build something and to try to put it out there even if you stumble pretty mightily along the way.
turns.zh:
对我来说，Quibi最神奇的地方在于它重新点燃了我对这个行业的热情，重新激发了我做这份工作的热情。我是在2018年12月离开前任公司的，当时我觉得自己可能已经不适合继续做软件开发了。我从事这个行业已经25年了，经历了诸多变化。当时我觉得自己对这份工作的热情已经远不如十年前了。或许是时候开启人生的新篇章，尝试一些完全不同的事情了。（00:19:23）我当时列了一长串可能想尝试的职业：做糕点师、风景摄影师、在SoundCloud上发布劣质音乐……但这些想法都有一个共同点——我对它们一无所知。别人会问：“你想当糕点师？你会烘焙吗？”我回答：“不，我对烘焙一窍不通。”“你喜欢风景摄影？你会拍照吗？”我说：“不，我根本不拍照。”但我当时对这些兴趣满满，甚至在接受Techwrench采访时，当被问及离开Snapchat的决定时，我直言不讳地说：“我要彻底离开，另辟蹊径。”这个故事广为人知。但离开Snapchat几个月后，Meg Whitman和Jeffrey Katzenberg找到了我，他们当时正筹备New TV项目。（00:20:15）他们的提案是，尝试将移动互联网、硅谷科技和消费级技术的优势与好莱坞式内容制作相结合，打造专为手机端打造的定制化内容平台。他们既需要技术领导力，也需要产品领导力，问我是否有兴趣参与其中。尽管我当时几乎不接这种电话，但能与这两位共进午餐的机会实在难得。（00:20:50）我听完他们的提案后礼貌地拒绝了，说自己要去当糕点师之类的。这种对话每隔几个月就会重复一次，持续了七个月。我们共进午餐，他们向我汇报进展，我每次都拒绝参与其中。直到那年年底，我又去吃了一顿午餐，Meg解释说他们找来人负责技术和产品部门。（00:21:26）这两人离职的原因与Quibi本身毫无关联。他们分别在入职六周后离开。Meg说：“我们筹集了大量资金，向全世界宣称将在一年内推出产品。现在任务繁重，真心希望你能来帮忙。”我说：“我会每周花几天时间帮忙，但绝对不会两天。”她说：“不行。”
她说：“就周三晚上六点，关掉你的Quibi笔记本电脑，然后告诉自己，他们付钱给我的只是周二和周三的费用，周二早上再重新打开它。就这么简单。” 嗯，她说的大部分话都是对的，但这件事她错了。我一下子就深陷其中了。从零开始组建团队，从零开始设计和打造产品，真是太有趣了。（00:22:58）我们可以充分利用过去15年来涌现的现代软件架构技术。Quibi项目的某些情况确实让我感到尴尬，但我非常感激这段经历。我再次深深爱上了这个行业，也再次意识到，打造出一个产品并努力将其推向市场，哪怕一路上会遭遇重重挫折，其中的满足感也是无与伦比的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there something that you took away from that experience that taught you what to try to avoid? What to try to pull towards?
turns.zh: 是否有从那段经历中获得的启示，让你明白应该避免什么，又该如何把握机遇？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: I think I misunderstood or misjudged companies sometimes by thinking about them really focused on the product execution. If you find an interesting problem that people care about and you solve that problem in a really beautiful, elegant, delightful way, that's 10 times better than anything else that they can get in that same space, they'll tell their friends and all the rest will take care of itself. That was always my ambition. (00:24:16): Find a thing that I cared about building, do a great job building it really delightful way. Go really deep on listening to people and their feedback and iterate your way to success and breaking through that membrane that we all strive to get across. The really great word of mouth. But I think the thing I've come to better appreciate is that companies are also like a math problem that describes how you take investment and pour them into the equation and out the other side comes returns on some time horizon. (00:24:54): Yes, there are variables in that equation that are influenced by the product that you build and all of the little details and decisions that you make about making that product great. But if the equation is fundamentally broken or a big swing in and of itself, no amount of iteration and execution can get you out of the failed outputs of the broken equation. I think Quibi made a bet that you could build an entirely bespoke content library that was sufficiently scaled to get people to subscribe and retain for a couple billion dollars. It was a huge amount of money. But we made 70 shows in 18 months, which is more content than all of the major broadcast networks combined made in a single year. It was a pretty major accomplishment. We made a bet that we would augment those sort of-
turns.zh:
我觉得自己有时会误解或错误判断一些公司，认为它们过于专注于产品执行。如果你能发现一个人们关心的有趣问题，并以极其出色、优雅、令人愉悦的方式解决它，那比同领域其他任何产品都要好十倍。人们会把它推荐给朋友，其余的自然水到渠成。这始终是我的抱负。（00:24:16）：找到自己热爱打造的东西，以令人惊喜的方式把它做好。深入倾听用户反馈，不断迭代，最终突破我们都渴望突破的壁垒。获得口碑传播。但我逐渐意识到，公司其实就像一道数学题，如何将投资注入等式，最终在某个时间节点获得回报。（00:24:54）：没错，这个等式中的变量会受到你所打造的产品、产品细节以及优化决策的影响。但如果等式本身有根本性缺陷，或存在无法克服的波动，再多的迭代和执行也无法扭转失败的结果。  
Quibi曾押注打造一个完全定制的内容库，规模大到足以吸引用户订阅并留存——耗资数十亿美元。这笔巨额资金投入下，我们在18个月内制作了70部节目，内容量比所有主流广播网一年的产出总和还要多。这确实是相当了不起的成就。但我们也押注于借助这些内容——

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: And we made a bet that we would augment those sort of episodic and serialized or Hollywood style shows with a bunch of daily content that we produce at the level of network television, nightly news, and so forth, that would be an alternative to some of the sort of daily content that you might otherwise get on YouTube. And that was going to be about a third of the content spend. (00:26:26): One super interesting thing that no one talks about is that all of that content was designed to be made day of or day before it aired, so there was no back catalog of it. And it was all designed to be shot in these professional studios that we built out. It was really expensive, like I said, it was like a third of the investment we were going to making content, almost half the investment we were going to be making content. (00:26:51): And we launched two weeks into Covid and we couldn't make any of that content, except literally in the garages of the host's homes. And so we had this thing that was supposed to seem really set apart from YouTube, that literally now was being made exactly YouTube content, which is sort of like self-produced at home with very little sort of the support infrastructure of Hollywood. Now, you can argue, I think the content on YouTube is really, really exceptional in this category, and maybe we were never going to do better than that. (00:27:26): But I think what was really fundamentally broken with Quibi was that the actual foundational equation of can you make enough premium content that's totally bespoke and made for the service and takes advantage of the nature of the phone, it is enough content to get people to sign up and retain, and can you do that for a couple billion dollars? And I think the answer is no. The library has to be much, much bigger, and you have to have, like any company, you have to have sufficient time and energy to iterate on the content format itself, because our roadmap really wanted to innovate on the content format. (00:28:06): And so I think part of what happened is pretty quickly it became clear that the math was just wrong. It wasn't going to take 2 billion, it was going to take 6 or 8 or 10 billion. And the risk reward profile of betting 10 billion on the format was just more than anyone could stomach.
turns.zh: 当时我们打赌，要用一系列每日更新的内容——这些内容的制作水平要达到电视网电视、晚间新闻等节目的标准——来丰富那些传统的剧集式和系列化内容，或者说好莱坞风格的节目。这类内容将成为YouTube上日常内容的替代品。这些内容的制作预算将占总投入的约三分之一。  (00:26:26)：有个非常有趣但鲜为人知的细节是，所有这些内容都是在播出当天或前一天才制作完成的，因此没有任何存档内容。所有内容都是在我们专门搭建的专业摄影棚里拍摄的。正如我之前所说，这笔投入占我们内容制作预算的三分之一，甚至接近一半。  (00:26:51)：但新冠疫情爆发两周后，我们无法制作任何内容，只能在主持人家的车库里拍摄。原本定位与YouTube截然不同的平台，现在却在生产与YouTube非常相似的内容——即由普通人居家自拍、几乎没有好莱坞级制作支持的内容。当然，你可以说YouTube在这一领域的内容确实非常出色，或许我们永远也无法超越它。  (00:27:26)：但我认为Quibi的根本问题在于：你能否创造出完全为该平台量身定制、充分利用手机特性的优质内容？这些内容是否足以吸引用户注册并留存？而这需要数十亿美元的投入。答案显然是否定的。内容库必须大得多，而且像任何公司一样，必须有足够的时间和精力来迭代内容格式，因为我们的路线图本就希望在内容格式上进行创新。  (00:28:06)：所以我认为问题很快就显现出来了：整个商业模式的数学公式根本就是错误的。不只是需要20亿美元，而是需要60亿、80亿、100亿。用100亿去赌这个模式的风险回报实在是太高了，超出了任何人的承受范围。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I really like this metaphor and this mental model of the math formula of the entire business and thinking of it that way. I knew Covid changed the way people consumed content and that hurt. Quibi I think it was meant to be on the go, not sitting at home where you could watch anything you want. But also the fact that the content couldn't be made as well, as you were hoping to make.
turns.zh: 哇。我真的很喜欢这个比喻和整个商业模式的数学公式思维模型。我知道新冠疫情改变了人们的内容消费习惯，这确实带来了影响。Quibi原本定位是移动端内容，而不是人们可以随心所欲观看的居家娱乐平台。但内容制作质量未达预期，这确实是个问题。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: Yeah, for sure.
turns.zh: 是的，确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As a CPO, one of the biggest challenges is pushing back, trying to convince the founders of their mistakes, of doing what they want and just powering through it and dealing with it sometimes I guess is there anything you think you could have done looking back, or was the math formula set up for failure from the beginning and it's probably just not going to work out almost no matter what you did?
turns.zh: 作为首席产品官，最大的挑战之一就是反驳创始人的错误观念，试图说服他们改变策略，避免一意孤行。有时候你不得不面对现实：回过头看，你觉得本可以采取哪些措施？或者说这个商业模式从一开始就注定失败？无论如何努力都可能难以成功？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: One of the bets was that we weren't going to just use the apparatus of Hollywood to make the content. In part, we are going to use the apparatus of Hollywood to market the content. So Jeffrey had recruited this incredible Rolodex of literally the world's most famous celebrities to make shows for Quibi. We kind of had everyone either made something for launch or was going to make something. (00:29:42): And part of what they're going to do is turn up in culture and talk about their shows. We've heard a lot in the last six months about how hard it's to market movies because the stars can't go out and talk about the movies during the strike. (00:29:54): There was this theory that you could apply the marketing technique of Hollywood to get 20, 30 million people into the theater on opening weekend for Quibi. And that was always a very, very audacious take, I thought. Uber has all the money in the world to experiment with paid user acquisition, and they're not consistently a top 10 most downloaded app in the app store. (00:30:26): But the theory of Quibi, the math of Quibi, did require us to from day one land in the top 10 and stay there forever. The model would have worked if we could do that. And to the Hollywood marketing apparatus, the numbers that it takes to get there felt kind of small. If you can get 20 million people in to see Shrek on opening night new IP, surely you can get them to take their phone out of their pocket and download this thing and start a free trial. (00:30:54): Now, those of us who have spent our life in Silicon Valley making software and really, really tried to get people to show up and download new IP in large numbers know just how hard that is. (00:31:09): So maybe if I critique my own contribution to the math equation, maybe I should have beat the drum a little harder about just how unlikely it was that we were going to land the kind of distribution in month one that the model sort of required. If I had to go back and do it again, I think I would spend maybe more time investing and illuminating that aspect of the digital universe.
turns.zh: 其中一个赌注是，我们不会仅仅利用好莱坞的资源来制作内容。部分上，我们还将借助好莱坞的资源来推广这些内容。因此，杰弗里招募了全球最知名的名人阵容，为Quibi制作节目。我们几乎让每位名人都为Quibi的上线制作了内容，或者承诺会参与制作。（00:29:42）他们计划在文化领域露面，为自己的节目造势。过去六个月里，我们听闻许多关于电影营销难题的讨论——因为罢工期间，明星们无法外出宣传影片。（00:29:54）有人提出，可以借鉴好莱坞的营销策略，让Quibi首周末吸引2000万至3000万人进影院观影。我认为这个想法相当大胆。优步有充足资金进行付费用户获取尝试，但它却未能持续跻身应用商店下载量前十名。（00:30:26）Quibi的商业模式要求我们必须在首日便跻身前十，并长期保持这一位置。若能做到这一点，模式本应奏效。但相较于好莱坞的营销机器，Quibi所需的用户量显得微不足道。如果能让2000万人首日观看《怪物史瑞克》这种新IP影片，肯定也能让他们掏出手机下载Quibi并开启免费试用吧。（00:30:54）但在硅谷深耕软件行业、深知让大量用户下载新IP有多难的我们深知这绝非易事。（00:31:09）所以，如果要批评自己在数学模型中的贡献，或许我本该更强调首月获得模型所需规模的分发量有多么困难。若能重来，我会花更多时间深入剖析数字世界的这一层面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such a good takeaway of just showing the leaders, here's the data, here's the assumptions that we're all betting on, and do you believe this can happen? And they probably would've said, "Yes, this will happen. I'm so confident."
turns.zh: 这真是一个绝佳的总结案例——向领导层展示数据，说明我们基于的假设，然后问他们是否相信这能实现。他们很可能回答：“没错，这一定能实现。我对此深信不疑。”

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: What made it hard was, it wasn't structurally impossible. If you had to be bigger than any app that had ever been made, then you could probably make the case it's impossible. But since you only sort of had the land in the top 10, you couldn't quite say it was impossible, you could just say it was highly improbable. (00:32:18): And maybe one of my mistakes was, I guess I imagined that we would launch, and when the likely thing happened that we got millions of people to download the app, which we did, and then when we inevitably struggled to retain those users at high percentages, and we retained at what I think of as a good industry starting point, but we weren't setting any records on retention. I just imagined that what would happen next is the thing that happens in all young companies, you would iterate. You would grind on the funnel until a year later, two years later, six months later, whatever it is. You figured the formula out to get people in and get them to stay and get them to retain. (00:33:12): And what I didn't appreciate was just how quickly you go back to the foundational math and then the math really says you just can't. You can't spend two years iterating your way on optimizing the funnels like you would in a startup that had a different cost structure. In a world where you have to spend a billion dollars a year of making content, you just can't afford to not be a hit.
turns.zh: 难点在于，这并非结构性障碍。如果你要打造一款比以往任何应用都更庞大的产品，那么或许可以宣称这是不可能的。但既然你只在前十名占据了一席之地，就无法断言这完全不可行，只能说可能性极低。（00:32:18）：或许我的失误之一是，我曾以为我们会一举成功。当数百万用户下载应用（我们确实做到了，但随后在用户留存率上遇到了挑战）时，我们本可以保持乐观，但实际留存率仅达到行业平均水平，远未达到行业标杆。当时我以为接下来会像所有初创公司一样，通过迭代优化。但我忽视了一个关键点：当你面对每年数十亿美元内容制作成本时，根本无法承受两年时间的优化迭代。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it's also important to just remind us, it's okay for these things to happen. People take a bet, as you said, we're going to try this thing, here's our bet, here's our experiment. We're betting on this sort of format in this business. We're going to raise money from investors that know they might lose all their money. And it sometimes doesn't work out. It's part of the game.
turns.zh: 我认为重要的是要提醒大家，失败并不可怕。正如你所说，人们会下注：我们要尝试这个模式，这是我们的赌注、我们的实验。我们押注于某种商业模式，筹集投资者的资金，明知可能血本无归。但有时事与愿违，这就是商业的游戏规则。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: It's certainly painful to take money from investors even if they know what they're doing and to not get them a return. I feel a real responsibility to investors to do better than we did at Quibi. (00:34:08): But yeah, I mean, there is a risk reward thing that goes along with these investments, and part of the reason they get all the riches on the upside is that they're going to bet on some Quibis along the way too.
turns.zh: 即使投资者深知风险，也不愿看到投资回报落空，这无疑令人心痛。我深感对投资者的责任重大，要比我们在Quibi的表现更出色。（00:34:08）：但风险与回报确实相伴而生，他们之所以能在上行中获取丰厚回报，正是因为他们愿意押注于Quibi这样的项目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So as you were talking, you said that it was called NewTV, and that sparked a memory, and I searched my email. And I actually got an email from a recruiter in 2018, we just kicked off a very special executive opportunity, the CPO at NewTV, a new venture in Los Angeles, with Jeffrey Katzenberg and Meg Whitman, raising a billion dollars, working with top talent. Are you interested in exploring this opportunity?
turns.zh: 你提到这个项目叫NewTV，这让我回忆起往事。我翻了翻邮箱，2018年确实收到过招聘邮件：洛杉矶新创公司NewTV正在寻找首席产品官，与杰弗里·卡岑伯格和梅格·惠特曼合作，融资10亿美元，汇聚顶尖人才。感兴趣吗？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: Lenny, Lenny, Lenny. Your story could have been so much different.
turns.zh: 莱尼，莱尼，莱尼。你的故事本可以大不相同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This could have been Thomas podcast. Lenny, tell me about what happened at Quibi.
turns.zh: 这本该是托马斯的播客。莱尼，讲讲Quibi的经历吧。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: I would take that free.
turns.zh: 我倒是挺想免费听听的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know. There's pros and cons. They even sent this whole PDF, a TV in your pocket, NewTV. Amazing. All right. I'm going to read through this and see what they pitched back in the day. (00:35:05): Okay, let's move on to things that worked out really well, let's call it notable successes, other products you worked on that worked out great. So I'll list a few of them. And maybe what might be helpful is just we'll just go through each one and share what you took away from that experience, a lesson you learned from working on those products. (00:35:23): The ones that come to mind for me are Snap, Pandora, Apple if we want to go there. Also, you built, I don't know exactly what you did there, but you worked on You Don't Know Jack, this game that I loved. I think if you're an elder millennial, you're just going to like, "Oh my God, I love that game." I don't even remember it exactly, but I just remember the visceral feeling of playing that game and it was so much fun. So that's cool. I didn't know that you worked on that. And then there's also Sonos, which you're on the board. (00:35:49): So whatever order you think might be most interesting, just going through those and what did you learn from that experience?
turns.zh: 我不知道。各有利弊。他们甚至发了一整份PDF文件，叫“口袋里的电视”——NewTV。太神奇了。好吧，我要通读一遍，看看他们当时提出了哪些方案。（00:35:05）：好的，接下来聊聊那些成果斐然的项目吧，可以称之为显著成功案例，或者说你参与过的其他出色产品。让我列举几个。或许更有意义的是，我们可以逐一回顾这些项目，从中汲取经验教训。（00:35:23）：我首先想到的是Snap、Pandora，还有苹果——如果要提的话。还有你参与的You Don't Know Jack这款游戏，我超爱的。我觉得如果你是千禧一代前辈，肯定会感叹：“天哪，我超爱这款游戏！”虽然我记不太清具体内容了，但记得玩这款游戏时那种身临其境的感觉，真的太有趣了。太棒了。我之前都不知道你参与过这个项目。还有你现在是Sonos董事会成员。（00:35:49）：所以你觉得哪部分最有趣，就按顺序讲讲，每个项目都分享一下心得。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: I worked at Apple in the interval where Steve was gone, John Skelly, that kind of period, so System 7, System 8, Power Macintosh, that whole era. And we were doing a lot. We shipped a bunch of great hardware. We transitioned the company from Motorola 68,000 CPUs to the Power PC architecture. (00:36:19): But, particularly in that transition, we really struggled to ship consumer software features. I mentioned that I wrote three LAN folders and some other consumer features in my first six months at Apple, and they shipped four years later, actually after I'd left the company. I was a little surprised they were still in the software repository even, candidly. (00:36:40): But I'll tell you that one of the things culturally about Apple in that moment was, at least I felt like, a person was really rewarded if they could make a kind of broad contribution across functions. So if you were a talented software engineer, but also a thoughtful product designer, and maybe also had interesting input on product marketing, that you could build a really great reputation inside the company by playing all of those positions a little bit day to day. (00:37:19): And so when I left Apple after four years, I look back on my time, I didn't ship as much software as I had hoped, and I felt like a little bit like a professional gadfly. I was six miles wide and a centimeter deep. (00:37:36): And I went to work for this company called Berkeley Systems. In addition to You Don't Know Jack, they made a flying toaster screensaver, if you remember. You remember the nineties?
turns.zh: 我是在史蒂夫离开、约翰·斯凯利接手的那个时期在苹果工作的，System 7、System 8、Power Macintosh那个时代。我们做了很多事。推出了很多优秀的硬件产品，还把公司从摩托罗拉68000处理器过渡到了Power PC架构。（00:36:19）：但特别是在这个过渡阶段，我们在推送面向消费者的软件功能时遇到了很大挑战。我提到过，我在苹果的前六个月写了三个局域网文件夹和其他一些面向消费者的功能，结果四年后才发布——实际上是在我离开公司之后。我甚至有点惊讶它们还在软件库里呢。（00:36:40）：但我要告诉你，当时苹果的文化是，至少在我看来，如果你能跨职能做出广泛贡献，就会得到重奖。比如，如果你是个有才华的软件工程师，同时又是个有想法的产品设计师，或许还能对产品营销有有趣的见解，那么你就能在公司里树立很高的声望，每天在不同岗位上发挥作用，逐步积累口碑。（00:37:19）：所以四年后我离开苹果时，回顾自己的时光，我觉得自己没能推出足够多的软件，感觉自己像个职业刺客——面面俱到，却又一无所成。（00:37:36）：后来我去了一家叫Berkeley Systems的公司。除了You Don't Know Jack，他们还做过一个飞行烤面包机屏保，你还记得吗？还记得90年代吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How could you forget that?
turns.zh: 怎么会不记得呢？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: And when I met them, they were picking off this game development for this trivia game, and were looking for someone to lead the technical team. And so I joined as technical director for the You Don't Know Jack franchise, managed a team of engineers, and it was a completely different culture than what I was used to at Apple. (00:38:11): It was certainly the case that I was welcome to weigh in on the game design or the marketing or some other aspect of the deliverables, but my job was to build the software on time with high quality, period. And if I did those things, I'd be rewarded. And if I didn't, I would not be successful. And no amount of insightful feedback on the gameplay or the packaging, or whatever else I might want to do, was going to benefit me and my career at all. (00:38:48): And it was such a blessing to be forced to go deep on something, because I spent a lot of time developing chops as an engineering manager, but I also wrote a ton of software. And that's really honestly when I became a software engineer. My college education was insufficient to get me there, and the amount of software I wrote at Apple was insufficient to get me there. But I came out of my Berkeley Systems You Don't Know Jack experience feeling like I could really hold my own technically in a way that just wouldn't have happened. (00:39:20): And so I do think that there's something to be said for a culture where there are swim lanes and people are encouraged to be really, really exceptional in their lane. And so I feel really lucky that I stumbled into You Don't Know Jack When I did. (00:39:36): And it was also, I mean, it was the first thing that I worked on that had just huge cultural awareness for a couple of years. I mean, it's crazy, they're still making sequels. It has been nearly 30 years, and there are versions of You Don't Know Jack that are in all of the stores, in the PlayStation store, in the Xbox store, in the iOS store. You can play new versions of You Don't Know Jack to this day. It's crazy.
turns.zh: 当时我遇到他们时，他们正在为这款益智游戏开发《你不知道的杰克》系列，正在寻找一位能领导技术团队的人。因此，我加入了《你不知道的杰克》系列担任技术总监，管理一个工程师团队。这与我在苹果公司习惯的文化截然不同。（00:38:11）：确实，我可以对游戏设计、市场营销或其他交付成果方面提出意见，但我的职责就是按时高质量地开发软件，仅此而已。如果我做到了这些，就会得到奖励；如果做不到，就无法成功。无论我对游戏玩法、包装或其他方面提出多么有见地的反馈，都对我的职业生涯毫无益处。（00:38:48）：被迫深入钻研某个领域对我来说是一种福音。虽然我在苹果公司担任工程经理期间积累了不少经验，但我也编写了大量软件。说实话，那时我才真正成为一名软件工程师。我的大学教育不足以让我达到这个水平，而我在苹果公司编写的软件量也不够。但从《你不知道的杰克》在Berkeley Systems的开发经历中，我感到自己在技术上能够独当一面，这在以前是无法想象的。（00:39:20）所以我认为，在一个有明确分工、鼓励人们在各自领域做到极致的文化中，确实有其价值。我很幸运能在那个时候接触到《你不知道的杰克》。（00:39:36）而且这也是我参与的第一个在数年内引发巨大文化热潮的项目。说起来真是不可思议，他们至今仍在推出续作。近30年过去了，《你不知道的杰克》的各个版本遍布各大应用商店——PlayStation Store、Xbox Store、iOS Store。直到今天，你仍能玩到新版本的《你不知道的杰克》。这太不可思议了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did not know that. I see the website now and it's a little different, but basically the same.
turns.zh: 真没想到。我现在看这个网站，虽然有点不同，但基本内容还是一样的。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: So I'd say my lesson from You Don't Know Jack was definitely, it really does pay to get good at something and not just be a generalist. (00:40:24): And then, I mean Pandora, it wasn't quite the next thing that happened. After You Don't Know Jack was Pets.com, and then after Pets.com there was nuclear winter in the industry and I worked in enterprise software for a while. (00:40:37): And after nuclear winter I had this idea that I was going to build a destination for music discovery on the web. And I've been doing enterprise software, the consumer intranet was non-existent for those years, early aughts. (00:40:54): But around 2004, things started to thaw a little bit and you started to hear the first signs of the companies that we came to call Web 2.0, Flickr would've been one of the early examples. And one of the enterprise software things I did was a personalization recommendation engine that used a vector space. It's like a lot of the things that we're talking about now in AI, albeit 20 years ago. (00:41:21): And so I knew something about recommendation systems in the enterprise space, and I was super passionate about music. I'm not a musician, but I was that kid in college who would corner you and be like, oh, if you like this band, I got to play this for you and [inaudible 00:41:37] with stereo until you would beg to leave. (00:41:40): And so I had this idea that maybe I can use the internet to do that at scale, not with just one person, but with hundreds of thousands of people or millions of people maybe. Introduce them to music that they would love but otherwise would miss out on. (00:41:53): And I promised that I was going to tell stories about luck in my career, there's been a gazillion of them. But one really dramatic incidence of that is I was sort of biding my time to exit this enterprise software company. I was VP of engineering, a whole team that reported to me. I felt a lot of responsibility to exit in a responsible way. But I was really excited about this digital music company that I was going to start. But I wasn't telling anyone at all because I didn't want ti to get back to the team. (00:42:25): So I flew down to Los Angeles to go out to Coachella in the spring of 2004, and completely randomly physically bumped into a guy that I had gone to high school with on the polo field, and hadn't seen him in a decade. And the thing that we had in common in high school was we loved music. And so I tell them the story of, I'm going to start this company to do personalized digital music on the internet. And he said, there's this woman I work with who just left our company to move to Oakland to work for this little company called Savage Beast that are also doing something in music recommendation. Do you want to talk to them? And I said, "Sure, why not?" (00:43:11): So I got introduced to Tim Westergren, who was the founder of Savage Beast. Savage Beast was like a seven or eight full-time employees at that point. They made a music recommendation engine that they licensed to other companies to put in consumer products. So Savage Beast's customers were Best Buy, who put it in kiosks, and AOL, who used it on the AOL Music website. And they were looking for a VP of engineering. And I got the offer, thought about it a little bit. I declined because it was kind of this B2B2C thing and I really wanted to do something consumer and I had an idea about the app. (00:43:49): And a month later, they called again and said, "We keep talking to people. We really think that you're the person." And interestingly, one of the reasons they thought that I was the person is they were really impressed by the fact that I had run engineering at Pets.com. So I mean, it's just one of those things where these things do pay dividends, even when they're a disaster. (00:44:07): And honestly, what I would really say was almost like a lapse in judgment, I said yes, even though it wasn't the product that I wanted to build. And I won't bore you with all of the details, but 90 days later, after some typical early stage founder drama stuff, the founding head of technology and product had resigned completely unrelated to my arrival. And the company had a new CEO, Joe Kennedy, and Joe had this idea for what he called the 1-Click Personal Radio. And Joe is a product marketer and just the best CEO in the whole world. We spent 10 years together building Pandora. (00:44:51): And he sort of gave me the keys and just said, "As long as it fits the brief for 1-Click Personal Radio, it's all yours." And I got to build the team and the culture, in collaboration with him and Tim the founder, over the course of the next 10 years, and just every good thing. (00:45:14): So I mean, there's just a million billion lessons from Pandora, and everything I am as a product leader and then an engineering leader comes from things that happen at Pandora. (00:45:24): But maybe the thing that I think of first is, I think we met our early audience in an incredibly genuine way. For example, when we launched the support@pandora.com was an alias for all@pandora.com. So if you sent a customer service request to Pandora, every single person in the company received it. And because we made a decision to have no customer support team in the first year, the expectation was that whoever sees the request first should respond to it. (00:46:01): And so you would write to us and you would get the founder or you'd get me or you'd get the engineer who wrote the feature or you'd get the CEO. And there were no macros to respond to commonly asked question. There was no read the FAQ. And there were no rules about what you could and couldn't say. If the person's like, "I think this feature is stupid and broken," we would encourage people to say, "You know what? I think you're right and I'm really struggling to get our stupid head of product to agree with me. I'm going to CC Tom and maybe we can convince him that this was a bad decision." (00:46:35): And we did all of that because we thought one of our superpowers as a young company was that we could just engage with our audience as real human beings, not as a shiny brand that was trying to be something that we could just never be. This period is where the iPod and iTunes are at the peak of their powers. And so there was no way we could sort of out-Apple Apple on the brand front. (00:47:02): And so we were just ourselves, and I think it really, really was a catalyst for the word of mouth that developed around Pandora. And we never spent any money on paid user acquisition, literally no dollars in the entire time I was there, because people loved the product and they told their friends about it and that's how it grew.
turns.zh:
所以我要说，从《你不知道杰克》中学到的一课就是，专注于精通一项技能而非成为通才，确实是值得的。（00:40:24）然后，我是说潘多拉（Pandora）并非接下来发生的事。在《你不知道杰克》之后，是Pets.com，接着是行业的寒冬期，我曾在企业软件领域工作过一段时间。（00:40:37）寒冬过后，我萌生了在网络上打造音乐发现平台的想法。那个时候我一直在做企业软件，而消费级互联网在千禧年初期几乎还不存在。（00:40:54）但2004年左右，行业开始回暖，你开始听到Web 2.0公司的萌芽迹象，比如Flickr就是早期例子之一。我当时做的一个企业软件项目是基于向量空间的个性化推荐引擎。这和我们现在谈论的AI技术有很多相似之处，虽然那是20年前的事了。（00:41:21）所以我对企业领域的推荐系统有所了解，同时又对音乐充满热情。我不是音乐家，但我在大学时就是那种会缠着别人推荐乐队、用音响播放直到对方求饶离开的家伙。（00:41:40）于是我有了个想法，或许能利用互联网大规模实现这种服务，不只是针对一个人，还能惠及数十万甚至数百万用户，让他们发现自己错过的优质音乐。（00:41:53）我答应过要讲讲职业生涯中的运气故事，类似经历数不胜数。但最戏剧性的一次是，我当时正耐心等待离开那家企业软件公司。作为VP of Engineering，手下有一整个团队，我觉得有责任以负责任的方式离职。但我对即将创办的数字音乐公司满怀热情，却从未向任何人透露过想法。（00:42:25）2004年春天我飞去洛杉矶参加科切拉音乐节，意外在高尔夫球场碰到高中同学，已经十年未见。我们共同的爱好就是音乐。于是我跟他讲了我的计划，要创办个性化数字音乐平台。他说他同事刚离职去奥克兰加入一家叫Savage Beast的小公司，专攻音乐推荐。想不想聊聊？我答应了。（00:43:11）于是我见到了Savage Beast创始人Tim Westergren。当时Savage Beast只有七八个全职员工。他们开发的音乐推荐引擎授权给其他公司用于消费级产品。客户包括百思买（Best Buy）和AOL。当时他们正招VP of Engineering，我考虑后拒绝了，因为那是B2B2C模式，而我更想做面向消费者的产品，还对某个应用有想法。（00:43:49）一个月后，他们再次联系我：“我们一直在找人，你就是我们要的人。” 有趣的是，他们认为我合适的原因之一是，我在Pets.com的经历。
他们对我在Pets.com负责工程部门的经历印象深刻。所以我的意思是，尽管这件事最终以失败告终，但它确实带来了回报。（00:44:07）：说实话，我当时的选择其实是个判断失误——尽管那不是我想打造的产品，但我还是答应了。我就不跟你们详细说过程了，但90天后，经过一些典型的初创公司创始人之间的闹剧后，技术和产品部门的创始人离职了，与我的到来毫无关联。公司换了新CEO乔·肯尼迪，他提出了一个叫“1键个人电台”的创意概念。乔是个产品营销天才，也是全世界最棒的CEO。我们一起花了10年时间打造Pandora。（00:44:51）：他把项目交给我，说：“只要符合1键个人电台的需求，尽情发挥吧。”接下来的10年里，我与他和创始人蒂姆合作，共同打造团队文化，一切都顺风顺水。（00:45:14）：Pandora给了我无数宝贵经验，我如今作为产品和工程负责人，很多能力都源自在Pandora的历练。（00:45:24）：但最让我难忘的是，我们以极其真诚的方式赢得了早期用户的信任。比如，support@pandora.com邮箱曾作为alias@pandora.com的别名存在。用户向Pandora提交客服请求时，公司所有员工都能收到。鉴于我们第一年没有组建客服团队，规则是第一个看到请求的人必须回复。（00:46:01）：用户给我们写信，回复者可能是创始人、我本人、负责该功能的工程师，或者CEO。没有固定模板应对常见问题，用户也不受任何言论限制。比如有人说“这个功能太烂了”，我们会鼓励他们说：“没关系，我也这么认为，但产品负责人就是不听。我把邮件抄送给汤姆，或许能说服他这是个糟糕的决策。”（00:46:35）：我们坚持以真实的人格与用户互动，不伪装成光鲜亮丽的品牌。当时iPod和iTunes正值鼎盛时期，我们根本无法在品牌形象上超越苹果。（00:47:02）：所以我们保持本色，我认为这正是Pandora口碑传播的催化剂。我们从未花钱购买用户，整个任期内没有投入一分钱，因为用户爱用我们的产品，会主动推荐给朋友，口碑自然增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I saw a stat that you grew Pandora from 0 to 80 million users, from 10 employees to 3000 employees, from 0 basically to a multi-billion dollar company.
turns.zh: 我看到一项数据：你们把Pandora从0用户发展到8000万用户，从10名员工扩展到3000名员工，从几乎零起点成长为市值数十亿美元的公司。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: We did those things. We did. (00:47:34): Also, I think my product stewardship in some ways set the scene for Spotify to walk through the digital streaming door and show us the exit. So Pandora is, again, such a privilege to be able to work on something that touched and continues to touch tens of millions of people's lives every month. But it's bittersweet from the standpoint that I think we had an opportunity that in some ways we misplayed.
turns.zh: 这些成就都是我们努力得来的。确实如此。（00:47:34）另外，我认为我在产品管理方面的努力为Spotify打开了数字流媒体市场的先机，让他们后来居上。我再次强调，能参与开发一个每月影响数千万人生活的产品，是一份莫大的荣幸。但从另一个角度看，这也令人心酸，因为我们曾有过一些错失的机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My mom is still a huge fan of Pandora, uses it every day for whatever choice.
turns.zh: 我妈妈至今仍是Pandora的忠实用户，每天都会用它来挑选音乐。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: I mean, it's still going. And the numbers are still tens of millions of people in the US listen every month. So it's a thing. But yeah, it's a little sad that it didn't have quite the staying power that some of these other things that have come along since have.
turns.zh: Pandora至今仍在运营，美国每月仍有数千万人使用它。所以它依然有其价值。但确实有些遗憾，它没有像后来出现的其他平台那样经久不衰。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just on that topic, do you think there's something that you could have done, someone could have done? Do you think there was an opportunity to become Spotify? Or is it the business model and the math formula was set up in such a way that it was near impossible?
turns.zh: 就这个话题而言，你觉得当时有没有可以改进的地方，或者本可以采取不同的策略？有没有机会成为像Spotify那样的巨头？还是说其商业模式和数据算法注定了难以复制？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: One of the things that was tough for Pandora was that when we started it, digital music was a category that no investor wanted to touch. It was lawsuits. There was no money to be made. There were relationships with the labels that were completely impossible to nurture. And there had been no big outcomes. I think the biggest exit in digital music when we got going was I think Yahoo had bought Musicmatch for like $400 million. And so that was seen as kind of the ceiling on the opportunity. (00:49:08): And along the way we found investors who believed in our vision and invested ultimately hundreds of millions of dollars in the company over its pre-public years. But there was never investor enthusiasm for the company in the category that was anything like the investor enthusiasm that a company like Spotify enjoyed just six, seven years later, Snap enjoyed for its pre-public tenure. (00:49:35): And I think part of what was different for Spotify is that the comps were not... Musicmatch was 400 million, they were Pandora at 8 billion, but even above that they were Netflix at 100 billion. And so investors just had this new sort of optimism about what you could do in subscription and in streaming, and Spotify really played that to their advantage in a way that we couldn't because we had gone public and the public market investors were still trying to figure us out. So we didn't have access to capital. It was very hard for us to take the same kind of risks that Spotify took. (00:50:17): But then I think we just completely misjudged one really important thing, which is that we were really inspired by disrupting terrestrial radio. Terrestrial radio is the predominant form of music consumption in the country. People spend, I can't remember the exact stats, but by minutes consumed, it's something like 10 times more music minutes a month on radio in the aughts and early tens than on owned music. And the advertising supported sort of radio market was a $30 billion category, and recorded music was $8 billion. (00:50:57): And so we had this idea that we're going to reinvent radio, and Spotify and Rdio and Apple Music and the 14 others, Rhapsody, which was Spotify before Spotify, they were all going to chase this smaller owned recorded music opportunity, and that we could be left relatively alone over here going after the less sexy but actually bigger market. And I think we just got it wrong. It should have been obvious that inevitably all of your music in any format was going to be delivered as a stream from the cloud. And that the record labels in particular, they were going to set the terms on what the structure was. And the structure that they preferred was the Spotify structure. And we operated under a different licensing...
turns.zh: 潘多拉（Pandora）最初面临的挑战之一是，当我们刚创立公司时，数字音乐领域根本没有投资者愿意涉足——到处都是诉讼，根本赚不到钱，与唱片公司的合作关系也难以为继，更别提取得重大成功了。在我们起步时，数字音乐领域最大的退出案例可能是雅虎以约4亿美元收购Musicmatch，而这被视为该领域发展的天花板。（00:49:08）：在此过程中，我们找到了相信我们愿景的投资者，他们在上市前为公司注资数亿美元。但该领域从未获得过与Spotify或Snap等公司在上市前获得的投资热情相媲美的关注。（00:49:35）：Spotify的成功部分在于，其可比公司（如Musicmatch估值4亿美元，潘多拉估值80亿美元）所处的市场环境完全不同——Netflix估值1000亿美元。投资者对订阅和流媒体服务前景充满乐观，而潘多拉因已上市且投资者仍在试探其价值，无法像Spotify那样灵活布局。（00:50:17）：但我们误判了一个关键点：我们曾受启发于颠覆传统广播电台。广播是美国主流音乐消费方式，数据显示，在2000年代初，广播音乐消费时长是付费音乐的十倍之多；广播广告市场规模达300亿美元，而付费音乐仅80亿美元。（00:50:57）：我们误判了市场方向：以为可以重塑广播模式，而Spotify、Rdio、Apple Music等14家公司（包括Spotify的前身Rhapsody）都专注于规模较小的付费音乐市场。结果证明，所有音乐格式终将通过云端流媒体传送，而唱片公司必然主导流媒体标准。潘多拉选择了政府颁发的法定授权许可，而Spotify则采用专有授权模式。我们本应预见这一趋势——所有音乐格式最终都将转向云端流媒体，而唱片公司必将主导流媒体标准。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: And we operated under a different licensing regime that they hated, that was a statutory license that we got from the government. And it would've been exceptionally risky for us to come out from under the statutory license and do direct deals with the labels, but it was a requirement to play in the world that they imagined as the future, and we should have imagined as the future, too. And eventually, the company got around to it, but it was too late.
turns.zh: 我们的授权模式与唱片公司矛盾重重，最终导致公司错失良机。我们本应预见，所有音乐格式最终都将通过云端流媒体传送，而唱片公司必将主导流媒体标准。我们本应预见，Spotify的成功将催生订阅经济的巨头，而我们却错失了先机。最终，公司虽有所调整，但为时已晚。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting that so much of this was rooted in that original vision that you shared of Pandora of the radio, smart radio in your pocket, [inaudible 00:52:37] personal radio that you just stayed on that track, even though there was this other track. But I think it's important to point out, you said it was seven years later. And I feel like there's this interesting trend with the companies you've worked at, pets.com and Pandora, that it's too early, you just come too early at these ideas. And I feel like that tells me Quibi might still happen. There's a Quibi coming seven years from now.
turns.zh: 很有趣的是，这一切都源于你最初对潘多拉的构想——将广播融入口袋智能设备，打造个人专属电台。尽管当时还有其他竞争方向，但你始终坚守这条道路。我觉得值得指出的是，你提到这个项目推迟了七年。而我注意到，你曾任职的宠物网（pets.com）和潘多拉（Pandora）这两家公司都面临一个共同的问题——创意来得太早，市场尚未成熟。这让我觉得Quibi或许仍有机会。七年后或许就会有新的Quibi问世。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: You know what's really funny about that? Just today, there's a headline about a Hollywood-produced show that's launching on Instagram Reels and TikTok that was shot vertical. And the headline is literally something like, "Is TikTok the new TV?" And it's pretty funny that literally, that's what Jeffrey and Meg called it when they were incubating the idea. I mean, I think it's pretty clear that purpose-built video for mobile looks a lot like TikTok. And I don't want to take anything away from all of the innovation in that space that they and the other players are driving that Quibi didn't capture in its initial product definition. But I mean, obviously, we stare at our phones consuming video of all kinds all day every day. So there there's definitely something there.
turns.zh: 最有趣的是，今天刚看到一则新闻标题：好莱坞制作的垂直拍摄短剧即将登陆Instagram Reels和TikTok平台。标题直译就是“TikTok会成为新电视平台吗？”这太巧了，因为杰弗里（Jeffrey）和梅格（Meg）最初孵化这个创意时，就将其称为"TikTok式电视"。我认为很明显，专为移动设备打造的视频内容与TikTok极为相似。我无意贬低其他创新者在该领域的努力——Quibi在最初的产品定义中确实未能捕捉到这些创新。但显然，我们每天都在手机上沉浸式观看各类视频内容，这背后必有深层逻辑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The PDF that I mentioned that I got from the recruiter, the first page again says, "You have a TV in your pocket." So it's exactly what they're pitching. That's amazing. All right. I think what I've learned, I need to bet all my money on this new Quibi clone because the timing might be right.
