turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: At Pandora, I was the head of product and was head of engineering. And our CEO was brilliant, but he was a product marketer. I mean, Joe was all things. He was an engineer by education, and a great marketer, and a great finance person, and just such a utility player at a very, very high level across every discipline. But he was also really, really good at letting his team do their jobs. He really let me run product and engineering. And so not only did I have tremendous latitude to make good and bad decisions about product, I also really got a seat at the table to help lead the company. So rewarding, so gratifying. Best professional experience that one could have. (00:56:05): So I leave Pandora after a decade. I take a year trying to figure out what I'm going to do next. But after about a year, I got introduced to Evan. And it's kind of a funny story. A mutual friend sent this introduction over. Evan immediately responded and said, "Why don't you come down to Los Angeles and have a coffee with me?" So I fly down. It's not clear if it's a job interview or what it is really. I mean, I was just lightly exploring things that were out there and was a big fan of what he was doing with Snapchat. So I spent 45 minutes with him, and then I spent 45 minutes with the head of engineering, and another 45 minutes with the head of legal, and then they tossed me into a conference room with a dozen product designers, all in their mid to late 20s, many of which had gone to school at Stanford with Evan. (00:57:01): I would come to learn all really, really, really impressive super, super talented people, but it was just 10 of us sitting around a conference table. And it wasn't really clear that they knew why they were talking to me, but we had an hour long free ranging conversation. And so I left, and I thought it was a totally fascinating morning, but I wasn't sure what had happened, really. It was like "Well, with these interviews, it all seemed very ad hoc. Is there a job opening?" It was a little odd. And I went to lunch on Abbott Kinney and got a text from Evan's admin saying, "Can you come back to the office? Have you gotten on your plane yet?" I was like, "I was just ordering lunch. I'll just come back right away." (00:57:49): So I go back. Now, it's one o'clock in the afternoon. This entire thing started at nine o'clock in the morning. I sit down in the conference room. Evan comes in with a manila envelope and says, " We loved you. We'd like for you to be our VP of product," and handed me a written offer, all the terms, the stock compensation, the whole thing. I'm gobsmacked. I'm flattered, that this is really playing to my ego. I can't believe that this company that feels like maybe the most interesting thing that's happening in consumer tech, that their notoriously brilliant and mercurial founder has taken enough of a shine to me that he wants to give at least some of the keys to the product kingdom over after such a short courtship. (00:58:34): So I leave, and when some of that buzz wears off, I start to wonder if there's some red flags here maybe. So I tell Evan, "Listen, I'd like to come back and meet more of the leadership team and spend more time with you, go a little deeper on what this means." And so we extend our courtship by another week or so, and I'm super impressed by the rest of the leadership team and the product thinkers and the designers and things that I was going to get to work with on a daily basis. And so I take the job full knowing that it's going to be wildly different than Pandora, where I had all of this latitude to do whatever I might want to do, and in the context of Snapchat, at best, I was going to be Evan's right hand, a person that principally executed his vision. (00:59:29): And that's certainly what it was. I mean, Evan and I ended up having a really great collaboration, but it was certainly most days, I was executing on his vision, both at a high level, and very much in the details. And Evan's truly brilliant, I mean, and he's also actually a really nice guy. I think in some ways, he gets a bad rep for... He has very high standards, but he's a very kind person, in my experiences with him. But it was a super exhausting job and not as soul satisfying as I wanted it to be. And after a couple of years, like I said, I thought maybe I just wanted to make croissants or something. (01:00:14): But one really, really big important lesson that I learned at Snap is about risk taking. And when you have the financial support and the foundational relationship with your investors that Evan has, it really allowed him to take these really big swings, acquire a technology that he thought was game changing, build features speculatively that maybe would be pruned in any other product roadmap planning process because the odds of them having an outsized impact were modest. And it just allowed him time after time to make bets that paid off, and we forget about the ones that don't work when there are so many home runs in those years. And we didn't have... Environmentally, we weren't set up for that at Pandora, but I think in some ways, I wasn't temperamentally inclined to those kinds of big swings. And I think I take bigger risks and encourage bigger swings now because of things I learned from Evan and Snap.
turns.zh:
在Pandora，我既是产品负责人，也是工程部主管。我们的CEO非常出色，但他本质上是一位产品营销专家。我是说，乔·蒙德拉克（Joe）是个全能型人才。他受过工程师教育，既是优秀的营销人才，也是出色的财务管理者，在各个领域都游刃有余。但他也非常善于放权，让团队自由发挥。正因如此，我在产品和工程管理上享有极大的自主权，不仅能自主决策产品策略，还能参与公司战略规划。这种体验令人振奋，是职业生涯中最宝贵的经历。（00:56:05）：在Pandora待了十年后，我离开了公司。接下来的一年，我试图理清未来的方向。大约一年后，经人介绍结识了埃文·斯皮格尔（Evan Spiegel）。故事有点趣味，一位共同的朋友转发了介绍邮件。埃文立刻回复道：“你何不来洛杉矶和我喝杯咖啡？”于是我飞往洛杉矶。当时并不清楚这是面试还是其他什么目的。我只是在探索机会，而且我一直很欣赏他对Snapchat的创新理念。和他聊了45分钟后，又分别与工程部主管和法务部主管各聊了45分钟，最后被带进会议室，与十几位产品设计师展开讨论（多数人与埃文同窗斯坦福大学，年龄普遍在25至30岁之间）。

（00:57:01）：我逐渐意识到这些人才令人惊叹，但整个面试过程相当随意。“这里有职位空缺吗？”我心存疑虑。午餐时收到埃文助理的短信：“能回办公室吗？你登机了吗？”我回复：“刚点餐，马上回。” 

（00:57:49）：回到办公室已是下午1点，而整个面试始于上午9点。我坐在会议室里，埃文拿出一个牛皮纸信封：“我们很欣赏你，希望你担任产品副总裁。”递给我一份书面录用通知，详细列明条款、股票奖励等。我目瞪口呆。这份认可极大满足了我的虚荣心——难以置信，在消费科技领域最具创新力的公司里，埃文这位以特立独行闻名的创始人，竟如此赏识我，短短几周便授予我产品帝国的部分掌控权。

（00:58:34）：离开Pandora后，冷静下来后，我开始怀疑是否存在隐患。于是我向埃文坦言：“我想再见见高管团队，深入了解职位内涵。”我们又延长了沟通期。一周后，我被整个领导团队、产品思维者和设计师们的才华深深折服，最终决定接下这份与Pandora截然不同的挑战。
无论我当时想做什么，尤其是在Snapchat的语境下，我最多不过是埃文的得力助手——一个主要执行他构想的人。（00:59:29）事实也确实如此。我和埃文最终合作得非常愉快，但大多数日子里，我都在执行他的构想——无论是宏观层面还是细节部分。埃文确实才华横溢，而且为人非常友善。在与他共事的过程中，我发现他虽然标准极高，但本质上是个善良的人。不过这份工作实在令人精疲力竭，远没有我期望的那么有成就感。几年后，我像说的那样，觉得自己或许更想去烤些可颂面包之类的。（01:00:14）但我在Snap学到的最重要的一课，是关于冒险精神。当你像埃文那样获得资金支持，与投资者建立稳固的关系时，这让他有条件去大胆尝试。比如收购一项他认为能改变游戏规则的技术，投机性地开发一些可能在其他产品路线规划中被砍掉的功能，因为这些功能产生巨大影响的概率很低。但一次又一次的冒险最终都带来了回报。那些失败的尝试在成功的光环下往往被忽视。而在Pandora，我们的环境并不支持这种冒险行为，从某种程度上说，我也缺乏这种大胆尝试的性格。不过现在，我从埃文和Snap那里学到了东西，变得更愿意承担风险，鼓励大胆尝试了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an awesome story. It resonates a lot with what Brian shared about how he thinks about product now and just telling people what to build versus very bottom up, "Tell us ideas you have." That impact, the way you run, we're going to talk a bit about you as CEO now, but I guess, do you have a place that you try to be of CEO as, "Here's what we're building"?
turns.zh: 真是个精彩的故事。这与布莱恩分享的他如今如何看待产品，以及从"告诉人们该做什么"到自下而上的"让我们听听你的想法"这样的转变，产生了强烈共鸣。那种影响力，以及你运营的方式——虽然我们现在要谈谈你作为CEO的角色，但我想问，你是否有过作为CEO，试图掌控所有细节，却忽视了让优秀人才自由发挥的阶段？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: As a product-oriented CEO, how much you should lean in to the details versus set direction and create an environment where great people can do great work, I suspect there's not one answer that applies to every company stage. When I was at Apple, one of the reasons that we struggled to ship things is that Apple did a great job of assembling incredibly, incredibly smart and talented people. Just everyone around me at that early stage in my career was so, so inspiring. But one of the side effects of that is we would get in a room and we would turn over some problem or opportunity, and we would talk ourselves out of every good solution because it wasn't perfect. I used to joke that Apple was the only place in the world where a vote of a thousand to one was a tie because that one person would be so thoughtful in their critique that the other thousand people would be like, "Hmm, that's right, that's right." And even though there's been this huge consensus of what the right answer was, we would talk ourselves out of making decisions.
turns.zh: 作为以产品为导向的CEO，应该在多大程度上深入细节，还是设定方向并营造环境，让优秀人才能创造出卓越成果？我怀疑这并没有适用于所有公司阶段的统一答案。我在苹果工作时，我们之所以难以按时交付产品，部分原因在于苹果成功汇聚了极其聪明才智横溢的人才。在我职业生涯早期，那些同事都极具启发性。但这种人才聚集的副作用是，我们每次开会讨论问题或机遇时，总能把所有好方案否决掉，只因它们不够完美。我曾调侃说，苹果是唯一一个千人投票仍形成平局的公司，因为那位持批判意见的人会用如此周密的分析，让其他千人折服道："嗯，有道理，有道理。"即便已经达成了共识，我们还是会自我否定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That one wasn't Steve Jobs, necessarily? It could be somebody else?
turns.zh: 那个人不一定是乔布斯吧？可能是其他人？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: He wasn't there.
turns.zh: 他当时不在场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: So I think what broke Apple out of that mode was Steve came back and they didn't vote anymore. Steve was just making the call. And so I have some sympathy for Brian and Evan, who have these big, thousands of people working for them. And as they delegate, they grow frustrated that there's not progress at the pace that they're looking for, and that there's indecision, and the people on the teams report that there's just churn and no progress, and there's fiefdoms and politics and all the rest, and that as the CEO, as a brilliant product-oriented CEO, they are uniquely situated to come in and cut through all of that garbage and get the trains running on time again. (01:03:49): Having said all of that, I also think that it can be a mistake to be that kind of leader in a smaller org because part of the opportunity in a small org is to assemble a group of people that are incredibly talented that believe in your mission and where who you can easily influence with a much lighter touch and set them up to build a culture in an organization that can execute. And so I see my job as CEO is to try to surf that edge of I'm really in the details. So I deeply understand the business and the product decisions that we're making and the processes that we're using to run the business, but not overplay my hand with respect to dictating outcomes. (01:04:40): The one thing you'll always have as CEO is, no matter how much you tell the team that when I swing by their virtual desk and say, "I've been thinking about this little detail that's not important right now, but what do you think?" It's like nine out of 10 times, that person is going to go and start working on that thing. And so you do have to be just really careful about the way you engage in some of those details, I think.
turns.zh: 所以我认为，让苹果摆脱这种困境的，是乔布斯回归后不再投票表决。乔布斯只需拍板决策。这让我对布莱恩和埃文深有同感，他们手下有数千名员工。随着权力下放，他们愈发沮丧于进展缓慢、犹豫不决。团队成员反馈只有混乱、无进展、各自为政、勾心斗角。作为CEO，作为杰出的产品导向型CEO，他们理应挺身而出，清除这些乱象，让列车重新准时开动。（01:03:49）说了这么多，我也认为在小型组织中当这种领导者可能是个错误，因为小型组织的机遇之一，就是能汇聚一群才华横溢、认同使命、易于影响的人才，让他们在组织中建立执行文化。因此，我认为CEO的职责是把握好尺度，既要深入了解业务和产品决策，掌握运营流程，又不能过度干预结果。（01:04:40）作为CEO，无论你怎么强调，当你走到员工虚拟办公桌前，说"我一直在思考这个现在不重要的细节，你怎么看？"十有八九对方会立即着手处理。因此，在处理某些细节时，真的要非常谨慎。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a really good episode I had with Lane Shackleton from Coda, and he shared this framework called flash tags that they use at Coda, and I think it comes from HubSpot, of you tell people, "Here's what the subpoena is. Is it an FYI? Is it a suggestion? Is it a do this?" There's four of them and one's like, "I will die on this hill. You need to do this."
turns.zh: 有一期节目，我和Coda公司的Lane Shackleton聊得很愉快。他分享了一个叫做“闪光标签”的框架，Coda公司正在使用这个框架。我觉得这个框架源自HubSpot。具体来说，你需要告诉别人：“传票内容是这样的。这是告知信息吗？是建议吗？还是要求必须执行？” 总共有四种表达方式，其中一种是：“我一定要坚持到底。你必须这么做。”

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: I try to do a lot of that. I wish I could say that in my experience that that pays off. I spend an awful lot of time, even the stuff I say very clearly, just one person's opinion, focus group of one, "Don't change your priorities to go work on this," it has more of an outsized impact on people's behavior than I intended.
turns.zh: 我也经常这么做。但说实话，我觉得这种做法效果不佳。尽管我花了大量时间，甚至把自己的观点说得很清楚，但往往只有一个人会听。就比如我说：“别为了做这个而改变优先级。” 但这对人们行为的影响远超我的预期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Easier said than done. Coming back to your journey, we've talked through the story up until getting to Quibi, but two years ago, you went in a whole new direction, and you're now the CEO of a company called Zero. What is it like to move from just being a product leader or engi leader at a company to being the CEO for the first time? Why did you choose Zero as that role? And what have you learned as CEO that you wish you knew as a product leader or engi leader at a company that listeners might find useful?
turns.zh: 是啊，说起来容易做起来难。回到你的职业发展历程，我们之前聊到你加入Quibi，但两年前你又转向了全新的方向，现在担任Zero公司CEO。作为产品负责人或工程负责人，首次担任CEO是什么样的体验？你为什么选择Zero来担任这个角色？作为CEO，你有哪些心得希望与听众分享，这些经验对产品负责人或工程负责人会有所启发吗？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: It's been a really, really incredible couple of years. In the aftermath of Quibi, I spent a lot of time, as we all do, soul-searching about what I learned and what I might want to do next. And as I thought about it, I realized that I really wanted to move on to something where I can have a direct impact on the culture and values of the company that I was involved in. I really got that opportunity at Pandora in a big way. And I had spent the five years of Snapchat and Quibi working for Evan and Meg and Jeffrey who are all incredible business leaders, but have their own very specific style and approach, and that leaves a mark on the culture that's unique to the founder. (01:07:04): And then as we've discussed, I'm always really interested in building things that are near and dear to me, and I was particularly thinking about what can I do that could have a really positive impact on the world in my next chapter. I've built an awful lot of media stuff through the years, video games and streaming services and so forth, and it seemed like maybe there was something that had a little bit more weight to it that I could spend my time on. And so my first thought was I would start something, a company idea I was quietly workshopping for some months. And completely independent from all of that, it's eight months into the pandemic, and my own personal health was at an all time low. I was 50 or 60 pounds overweight, my cholesterol was in the red zone. I mean, I was out of breath climbing stairs, which is something that I had never encountered in my life before. (01:07:59): I'm a bit of a yo-yo dieter and I'm always critical of looking in the mirror, but I was never ever really worried about my health, my longevity, and suddenly, I was. And so my solution to that was to go really deep on metabolic health, just thousands of hours of podcasts and videos and glucose monitoring patches and Oura Rings and digital fitness gear and just to try to understand the things that impact health and longevity. And as much as I would like to report that what I learned is that there's some magic pill that you can take, maybe some off label rapamycin or something, the truth is, is that to live a longer and healthier life, you really have to attack what I would call metabolic disease, which will manifest in overweight and obesity and pre-diabetes and diabetes and high cholesterol and all of these things that impact your long-term health. (01:08:59): And so I found Zero in this path and was using it to help with my own health journey. And Mike Maser founded the company four and a half years ago, and he and I were talking in this interval about my own experience with the product. I was just giving him product feedback and so forth, and he was telling me a little bit about his own entrepreneurial journey. And somewhere in the conversation, Mike said, "My intention is to step up into the executive chair role and to find a CEO for the company." So again, in my story, just over and over and over, this incredibly fortuitous thing happened. I just knew immediately that it ticked all the boxes, "Here's a chance to lead something that already had some momentum to impact the culture and values in a really direct way and was really, really close to my own personal journey." (01:09:50): And so we know we've got a great little company and 27 people, we've got more than a million users on the platform every month. Over a hundred thousand of them pay us with tens of millions of dollars of revenue through the years, and have had double-digit growth even coming out of the pandemic when lots of health and fitness companies saw retreats. And most importantly, it actually works. 75% of the people who use the platform lose weight. People lose, on average, five to 10% of their body weight in the first 60 days. And because of the success that people have, we grow just completely organically. We have no paid user acquisition at all. It's really a word of mouth business. (01:10:31): But that's not to say that it's not challenging. All startups are challenging. And what we've really focused on for the last couple of years is we've been really focused on unit economics, really trying to understand how much value can we derive and deliver for every person who downloads and installs the app, how do we convert them through all of the funnels efficiently and get them engaged with the product and get them to retain and drive that up in a really systematic way. And with my whole career, I'm definitely a person who started off thinking software development was mostly an art form, you find brilliant visionaries who have a deep understanding of human behavior, and they craft solutions for problems that other people don't see, and they make them delightful, and they get all the little details right. And when you found product market fit for the art, then you optimize them through a really quantitative take. (01:11:34): And so I'm definitely a person that sees both sides of that left brain and right brain equation that's important in software. But here's the thing my eyes have really opened to in the last two years. While companies are definitely the software that they make and the products that they deliver and that there is an art and science to that, as I described, there is also, if you step back, there is an equation that describes the business. It talks about how you turn investment into returns. And I suppose if I had come up with finance and been a business major that maybe that's the way that I would've conceived of companies to begin with. So maybe it's a little embarrassing that I had to be 53 years old before, I think, the scales fell through my eyes and I was like, "Oh, companies are equations." (01:12:24): And so when we first started talking about lifetime value and customer acquisition costs and getting those two things balanced and just the thinking about the unit economics of the business, my natural instinct was to go immediately to the leaf nodes of the equation like, "Oh, what percentage of people do we convert from install to registered and from registered to trial," and these very way down at the bottom of all the funnels and to ask the product team like, "Let's try to optimize these." And in the process though of trying to understand where we could take the business as we optimize those various dimensions and trying to understand too which of the dimensions had the most leverage, I started building these ever more sophisticated models that describe the whole business. (01:13:16): I mean, in startups, you get to wear a lot of hats. And definitely a hat that I'm wearing that I didn't anticipate at all is I'm the full-time FP&A guy for Zero. And so I built this spreadsheet that aggregates data from all of our business intelligence tools and raw data from our subscription transactions and looks at all of our historical results and all of our expenses and spend and then could use that to predict future scenarios by manipulating all of these variables. And it's just not at all the way I ever thought about products before. And I know that you've got lots of listeners like, "This guy's an idiot. This is a fundamental way to contemplate product work." (01:14:05): But if there's anybody out there like me who thought of it as art first and then optimization in the details, it is really, really powerful to spend the time to create the model that describes the whole thing so you can identify what are the high leverage points to focus on. So been doing a lot of that at the company in the last two years and it's really starting to deliver incredible results. Like everything in life, I mean, you sign up for things so you can learn, and that's the big one for me in the last year.
turns.zh:
过去这两年真是令人难以置信。在Quibi项目结束后，我和大家一样花了大量时间反思自己学到了什么，以及接下来想做什么。当我仔细思考时，我意识到自己真正渴望转向一个能直接影响所在公司文化与价值观的领域。在Pandora，我得到了一个绝佳的机会来实现这一目标。而在Snapchat和Quibi的五年间，我为Evan、Meg和Jeffrey这样的杰出商业领袖工作，他们都有着独特的风格和方法，这也为公司文化打下了创始人特有的印记。（01:07:04）正如我们之前讨论的，我一直对开发与自己息息相关的项目充满热情。在考虑下一步时，我特别想知道如何能在人生的新篇章中为世界带来积极影响。过去几年我参与了许多媒体项目，如视频游戏和流媒体服务，但总觉得缺少某种更有分量的东西值得投入精力。于是我的首个想法是创办一家公司——这个项目我已经悄悄筹备了几个月。与此同时，疫情已持续八个月，我的健康状况急转直下——体重超重50到60磅，胆固醇指标严重超标。爬楼梯都会气喘吁吁，这是我从未经历过的状况。（01:07:59）我曾反复节食，也总是不满自己的外表，但从未真正担忧过健康和长寿问题。突然间，我意识到必须深入研究代谢健康问题。为此，我投入数千小时学习播客、视频，佩戴血糖监测贴片，使用Oura智能手环和数字健身设备，努力理解影响健康和寿命的因素。尽管我曾幻想存在某种神奇药丸，比如非标用途的雷帕霉素之类，但现实是，要想延长寿命、保持健康，必须从根源上解决代谢疾病问题——比如超重、肥胖、糖尿病前期、糖尿病、高胆固醇等，这些都会损害长期健康。（01:08:59）在这条道路上，我发现了Zero这个产品，并将其用于自我健康管理。四年半前，Mike Maser创立了这家公司。在此期间，我们探讨了我的产品使用体验。我不仅提供了产品反馈，还听取了他的创业历程。在交谈中，Mike提到：“我的计划是接任CEO职位，为公司寻找新的领导者。”就这样，在我的人生轨迹中，一次又一次的机缘巧合发生了。我立刻意识到这份工作完美契合了我的所有期待——既能领导一个已有发展势头的团队，又能直接影响公司的文化与价值观，还能紧密贴合我个人的奋斗历程。（01:09:50）如今，我们拥有一家由27人组成的优秀小公司，平台每月吸引超过100万用户，其中十万多人付费使用，历年营收达数千万美元，即便在疫情冲击下也能保持两位数增长。
许多健康与健身公司都遭遇了挫折。但最重要的是，这个模式确实有效。75%使用该平台的人成功减重。平均而言，用户在前60天内能减掉5%至10%的体重。得益于用户的成功，我们完全实现了自然增长——完全没有付费用户获取策略。这完全是口口相传的商业模式。（01:10:31）但这并不意味着挑战不存在。所有初创公司都面临挑战。过去几年，我们真正专注于单位经济学，努力理解每个下载并安装应用的用户能获得和贡献多少价值，如何高效地在整个转化漏斗中转化用户，让他们参与产品使用，并系统性地提高用户留存率。我的整个职业生涯中，最初认为软件开发主要是一门艺术形式——你会遇到对人类行为有深刻理解的杰出天才，他们为他人看不见的问题设计解决方案，让产品充满趣味，处理好每个细节。当产品与市场契合时，你再通过量化方法进行优化。（01:11:34）所以我绝对是那种能看到软件左脑与右脑方程式两面的人。但过去两年让我大开眼界。虽然公司确实由其打造的软件和提供的产品组成，存在艺术与科学的双重维度，但退一步看，商业本质上也是一个等式，描述如何将投资转化为回报。我想，如果我曾学过金融或主修商科，或许一开始就会这样构想公司。所以53岁才意识到这一点，有些许尴尬。（01:12:24）当我们最初讨论终身价值、用户获取成本，以及平衡这两者时，只考虑了叶节点数据，比如“从安装到注册，再从注册到试用的转化率”这些漏斗底层数据，并要求产品团队优化这些环节。但在优化各个维度、寻找最具杠杆效应的维度过程中，我们构建了越来越复杂的商业模型。（01:13:16）在初创公司，你需要身兼多职。其中一个完全出乎意料的角色是，我成了Zero公司的全职财务与分析人员。我搭建了一个电子表格，将所有商业智能工具的数据和订阅交易的原始数据整合在一起，分析历史业绩和各项开支，进而通过调整这些变量来预测未来情景。这与我以往对产品的认知截然不同。我知道听众中很多人会说：“这家伙真是白痴。这是最基本的
思考产品工作的一种方式。（01:14:05）：但如果有人和我一样，最初把它视为艺术，然后再去优化细节，那么花时间构建一个能描述整个事物的模型是非常非常有意义的。这样你就能明确需要重点关注的高杠杆点。过去两年里，我在公司做了很多这方面的工作，现在确实开始取得令人惊喜的成果。就像生活中的每一件事一样，我觉得参与其中，就是为了学习，而这正是我过去一年最大的收获。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really love that takeaway of as a CEO coming back to share, here's what you should be thinking about that the CEO is probably thinking about, as a product leader, you may not be, of trying to actually spend the time to think about the business model and understand it deeply because your founders are thinking about it all the time. And so if you're not, you're missing out on here's a way to influence them, here's a way to...
turns.zh: 真的很喜欢这种CEO回归分享的做法。这里CEO传递的信息是，你们应该思考他可能在思考什么。但作为产品负责人，或许你并不会这样做，因为创始人一直在思考这些问题。如果你不参与其中，就错失了影响他们的机会。这里有一种方法可以影响他们……

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: It's so funny too because it's a thing I suddenly understand something that mystified me through my entire career, which was I'd go to board meetings and the investors would ask these probing questions, but they were really never about the product and what the product did and what the product roadmap was and what the features were and what this... It all seemed to operate at this level that was almost completely independent of the details of the "what is the solution you put into the world", which as a product-oriented thinker, was just completely baffling to me. And I now realize that they were tilling the soil that I'm talking about, they were tilling. (01:15:39): It doesn't really matter what the screens are and what the features are. I mean, it certainly matters, but that there's another higher order way to look at a company, which is really about the optimization of this equation. And I think particularly, if you sit on 25 boards, it's probably a much more efficient way to evaluate how your companies are doing and where to spend your time and how to help by thinking about them abstracted up at that layer. So I will never stop thinking about software development as being an art form and I will never stop enjoying the days when I get to lean in on the details, but it's been pretty eyeopening.
turns.zh: 这也挺有趣的，因为我突然意识到一件困扰了我整个职业生涯的事——参加董事会会议时，投资者会提出一些尖锐的问题，但这些问题往往与产品本身无关，比如产品功能、路线图、特性等。这似乎是在一个与“你推向市场的解决方案是什么”几乎完全无关的层面运作。对于以产品为导向的思考者来说，这实在令人费解。现在我意识到，他们其实在奠定我所说的基础，他们在耕耘土壤。（01:15:39）：屏幕上的东西和功能特性固然重要，但更重要的是从更高层面审视公司，关注如何优化这个等式。我认为，尤其是当你参与25个董事会时，这样评估公司表现、分配时间和提供帮助的效率会高得多。如果你能从更宏观的层面思考问题，你会发现这才是关键。所以我永远不会停止将软件开发视为一种艺术形式，也永远不会停止享受深入钻研细节的日子，但这确实让我大开眼界。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other thing that stands out here, one is I think this is especially true for consumer subscription apps, which I've done some research on. And basically, they never work. There's Duolingo, there's Zero, which I didn't know how much scale you guys reached. My math here real quick. So you have a million users, a hundred thousand paying users. You charge at 10 bucks a month. I know there's a discount for an annual plan, but basically, you're making somewhere around a million dollars a month, which you don't have to confirm or deny it, but that's the math I just did, and that's crazy. So congrats. That's a rare successful consumer subscription app. It never happens.
turns.zh: 另外，这里还有一点值得注意：消费者订阅应用尤其如此，我对此做过一些研究。基本上，它们都不成功。比如Duolingo，Zero（我不知道你们的用户规模有多大）。让我快速算一笔账。假设有100万用户，10万付费用户，每月收费10美元。虽然有年度计划的折扣，但基本上，每月营收约100万美元（这部分你可以不予置评），但这确实是我的计算结果，太不可思议了。所以恭喜你们，这是罕见的成功消费者订阅应用，太难得了。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: And like I said, every startup is hard, and I never stop being surprised at the new hard things that pop up every day. But we're on a really great run. We've had a tremendous year, and I'm just so, so proud of the team we've assembled. They're incredible for the last.
turns.zh: 正如我所说，每家初创公司都很艰难，我每天都会对新出现的挑战感到惊讶。但我们目前势头正盛，过去一年成绩斐然，我为我们组建的团队深感自豪。他们太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Part of the reason you're so successful is exactly what you said. There's a huge focus on LTV/CAC, the math formula, because for these sorts of businesses, the crux of it is can you acquire people for less money than you need to spend?
turns.zh: 你们如此成功的部分原因，正如你所说。在LTV/CAC（客户终身价值/客户获取成本）等数学公式上投入巨大精力，因为对于这类业务来说，关键在于能否以低于成本的价格获取用户？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: One thing that's really fortunate for Zero is Mike Maser, who founded the company, and I have both been around the block long enough and enough times that we remember 2008, we remember 2000. And so in these moments in the pandemic, there were companies in our category that were raising hundreds of billions of dollars with the intention of throwing it at paid user acquisition. And we made a conscious decision to optimize the value of the organic traffic that we were getting and to drive our growth through LTV expansion rather than top of funnel expansion, which was candidly not in fashion in 2021, 2022.
turns.zh: 零号公司（Zero）能有今天的成就，离不开创始人迈克·马瑟（Mike Maser）的功劳。我们都经历过足够多的风风雨雨，深知2008年的金融危机和2000年的互联网泡沫的教训。在新冠疫情期间，我们所在的行业中有许多公司不惜动用数百亿美元资金疯狂砸向付费用户获取渠道，而我们却有意识地优化自然流量价值，通过提升用户终身价值（LTV）来推动增长，而不是一味追求用户获取量（top of funnel expansion）——坦白说，这种策略在2021、2022年并不受市场青睐。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: ... in 2021, 2022. It turns out it's much more in fashion these days as companies are called upon to be much more capital efficient than they were during the pandemic era. I guess I feel somewhat fortunate that my natural inclination as an entrepreneur is more in sync with the expectations of the market than it was for a while.
turns.zh: ……但如今这种策略显然更受欢迎，因为企业被迫比疫情期间更加注重资本效率。我想我算幸运的，因为我作为创业者的天性与市场期望更为契合，这点在过去一段时间里并非如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So you've probably had the longest career arc of anyone I've had on this podcast. You've worked at all of these different companies in a lot of different phases. You're still at it. And I'm curious what you've learned about how to maintain your mental health and avoid burnout essentially through this journey. You mentioned you take some time off. Is there anything else you found or is that a trick of just how to not burnout?
turns.zh: 好的，你可能是我在这个播客上采访过的人中职业生涯最长的。你曾在不同阶段、不同公司任职，如今仍在奋斗。我很好奇，在这段漫长旅程中，你是如何保持心理健康、避免职业倦怠的？你提到会给自己放假，还有其他心得吗？或者说这只是一种避免倦怠的技巧？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: Do you know this Japanese concept called Ikigai?
turns.zh: 你知道日本的“生き甲斐”（Ikigai）这个概念吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm. Yeah, but share it. Share it for folks that may not be familiar.
turns.zh: 嗯，知道，但能给我们解释一下吗？可能有些听众还不熟悉这个概念。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: So the idea is it's a Venn diagram and there are four spheres. There's a sphere that's labeled what you love. There's a sphere labeled what you're good at. There's a sphere labeled what the world needs, and there's a sphere called what you can be paid for, and where they all intersect is this Japanese idea, Ikigai. It's the intersection of what you're good at, what you love, what the world needs, and what you can be paid for. If you find that, it's Ikigai. And interestingly, your listeners should go and find this because there are interesting ways to label the other intersections, the intersections where all four don't come together. And what's really interesting is that the ones that are three but not four, I think because they're the ones that are close but not quite to this really satisfying thing. And so it's like when you find those, it's really easy to choose a job or to choose a path where you have three but not four, which is a really great recipe if you're feeling like there's something just out of your reach that's really important. (01:20:09): Anyway, it's a great framework to think about your life and your career. So to start, I'm incredibly lucky that it's all Ikigai for me. What I'm good at, what I love, what the world needs, what I get paid for, they have always overlapped. And a big part of it is just what I love is this world. I love software, I love building software, I love writing software, I love using software. People are like, "What are your hobbies?" I don't think I have any hobbies and I think about, "Well, what kinds of things do I do on the weekend for fun?" And it's like I'm teaching myself After Effects or something, which I will immediately forget, but it's just fun to go really deep on some piece of interesting software. (01:21:02): So I'm very lucky. And so I think that has been super sustaining for me. One of the reasons I've been able to do it as long as I have without really burning out is that just, it's what I do. And in some ways it's why I come back to it. It's easy to say, "I'm going to become a pastry chef," but left to my own devices, I use software, I make software. It's my hobby, it's my passion, it's all the things. (01:21:29): But a couple of thoughts about how one engages with their work. One thing is I'm really not a #hustling kind of leader. There was a woman that I worked with on the Finder just out of college that left a really big mark on me. My own style of work then, I think I mentioned my memory of flashing, blinking the folder animation was a 2: 00 AM kind of thing. I was 23 years old. I woke up at 11 o'clock in the morning. I went to the office, I screwed around and played video games in the Apple Arcade and went to a couple of meetings and had lunch and stood at the whiteboard and pontificated about some nonsense. And then about four o'clock every day I would start writing software and I would write software until 2:00 or 3:00 in the morning and then I would go out to dinner with people from the team in the middle of it and whatever. (01:22:29): And so it kind of looked like I spent 14 hours a day, six or seven days a week at Apple, and I was celebrated for this. There was lots of nights where I would work clear through the night and my boss would come in the next morning, he'd be like, "Are you still here?" And I'm like, "I'm still here. Look at this cool thing I did." And I got a lot of attention for that. And then there's this woman on the team who showed up every single morning at 8:30, sat at her desk, wrote a ton of great software, and every night packed her stuff up and left. And she contributed more than I ever did. And I don't think she got the same kind of recognition that I got because of the way she did the work. (01:23:11): And when we were building the team and culture at Pandora, I thought about her a lot and really made a point of saying that I just wasn't interested in performative contribution, that it's the work that matters and what I want to celebrate is if you can show up and do it and go home and have other things in your life, because I think that's a recipe for being able to do it on a sustained basis rather than burning yourself out. (01:23:38): I think there's some nuance in this. I think 22 year old me was always going to want to work through the night. And so I think creating space that that's okay too is important. And I think maybe in some ways at Pandora it was almost like that wasn't okay. It was like, "You should be taking more breaks. Why are you going this hard?" But I do try to create environments where people have a reasonable balance between their regular life and their technology life or room for that if they choose it. And I do think that that has through the years, has helped me keep at it, but I still work a lot of nights and weekends because I love it. It's what I do. (01:24:16): Here's the other thing. I got very, very lucky with the Pandora experience and got this outsized, probably inappropriate financial reward for being a part of it and gave me options that I never imagined that I would have. And so after 10 years I left and I didn't know what I would do, but I did really need a break. It was a really hard job and that was definitely a moment where I needed some time to recover. But I think if you had asked me on that first day, I would say, "I don't know why these people find success and then start another company right away. Why? There's so many things you could do in the world, why would you start another company? It's so hard." (01:25:02): And I was particularly in love with the idea that I had access to experience. I didn't really care about things, I didn't want a fancy watch or whatever, a car, but I wanted to see the world. And so I thought, "I'm going to just go and I'm going to live in London for three months, then I come back to San Francisco for a month. I'm going to go live in Mexico City for three months and I'm going to just have this life where I'm soaking up experiences." And after doing that for six months, the thing that I came to realize is that what I care about way more than experiences is relationships. If you're the person who is constantly on a plane seeking out some new experience, it's really hard to form and maintain intimate, satisfying relationships. (01:25:47): So I went back to San Francisco, I'm like, "I can't be all over the world if I want to be engaged with friends and like-minded people." And you know what people do on Monday morning? They go to work. And so if you want to be engaged with humanity, where they are on Monday morning is at work. And so more than I had the itch to build things, which I do very much have, I had the itch to collaborate, to be in the game with other people. So that was what took me to Snapchat, took me out of chasing experiences and took me back to building again. And then as we've already described, at a point I thought, "Well, I care about this collaboration, but maybe it doesn't need to be software that I'm creating in the world." And Quibi gave me a chance to fall back in love with that process again. And here we are, more software.
turns.zh:
我的意思是，这是一个维恩图，有四个圆圈。其中一个圆圈标注的是你热爱的事物，另一个标注的是你擅长的事物，还有一个标注的是世界需要的东西，最后一个标注的是你能获得报酬的事物。它们的交集处，就是日本的"生き甲斐"（Ikigai）概念。它是你的热爱、擅长、世界需要以及能获得报酬这四者的交集。如果你找到了这个交集点，那就是Ikigai了。有趣的是，你的听众应该去探索一下，因为其他交集点也很有意思，比如四个圆圈都未交集的地方。最有趣的是，那些三个圆圈相交但四个圆圈不相交的地方，往往是因为它们距离这个令人满足的交集点仅一步之遥。当你找到这些交集点时，选择一份工作或一条职业道路会变得容易得多——只要你有三个交集点而非四个，那就是绝佳的选择，尤其当你觉得有某个重要的东西近在咫尺却始终可望而不可及时。（01:20:09）总之，这是一个思考人生与事业的绝佳框架。首先，我非常幸运，我的生活完全是Ikigai的体现。我的擅长之处、热爱之事、世界所需以及能获得报酬的事物，三者始终重叠。很大一部分原因在于，我热爱这个世界。我热爱软件，热爱开发软件，热爱编写代码，热爱使用软件。人们会问："你的爱好是什么？"我觉得自己没有什么爱好。我会想："那周末我做些什么有趣的事呢？"结果发现自己在自学After Effects之类的软件，虽然很快就忘了，但深入探索某款有趣的软件总能带来乐趣。（01:21:02）所以我很幸运。我认为这对我的职业生涯非常有益。能坚持这么久而不感到精疲力竭的原因之一，就是这就是我的生活方式。这也是我回归初心的原因之一。人们常说："我要成为糕点师。"但如果放任自流，我还是会用软件、开发软件。这是我的爱好、激情和一切。（01:21:29）但关于如何投入工作的几点思考。首先，我不是那种急功近利的领导者。我大学刚毕业时在Finder团队共事的一位女性给我留下了深刻印象。以我自己的工作风格为例，我曾提到过一个记忆深刻的时刻——文件夹动画闪烁效果的制作。那是凌晨两点的事。我当时23岁，睡到上午11点，去办公室玩Apple Arcade游戏，参加几次会议，吃午饭，站在白板前高谈阔论一些无意义的东西。每天下午四点左右，我开始写代码，一直写到凌晨两三点，然后和团队成员共进晚餐，诸如此类。（01:22:29）看起来我每周六天每天工作14小时，但却因此受到了赞誉。很多夜晚我通宵工作，第二天早上老板会问："你还在这里？"我回答："我还在这儿。看看我做出的这个酷东西。"我因此获得了诸多关注。团队里还有位女士，每天早上8:30准时到岗，坐在办公桌前写出大量优秀代码，晚上收拾东西回家。
左边。她比我贡献得更多。我认为她没有得到和我一样的认可，因为她做事的方式不同。（01:23:11）：当我们在Pandora建立团队和文化时，我经常想起她，并特别强调我对表面功夫式的贡献不感兴趣，重要的是工作成果。我希望能庆祝的是，你完成工作后回家还能享受生活，因为我认为这才是能够持续坚持下去的秘诀，而不是把自己累垮。（01:23:38）：这里面有一些微妙之处。我22岁时总想通宵工作。所以我认为给人们这样的空间也是重要的。但在Pandora，人们似乎觉得这样做是不被允许的。他们会说：“你应该多休息一下。为什么要这么拼命？”不过我确实努力营造一种环境，让人们能在正常生活和工作之间找到合理平衡——只要他们愿意的话。我认为这些年来，这确实帮助我坚持了下来，但我仍然经常在晚上和周末工作，因为我热爱这份事业。这就是我的选择。（01:24:16）：还有一点。我在Pandora的经历非常幸运，获得了超出预期的财务回报，拥有了从未想象过的期权。10年后我离开时，虽然不知道未来会做什么，但确实需要休息一下。那份工作太累人了，确实需要时间恢复。但如果在第一天问我，我会说：“我不明白为什么有些人成功后就立马创办新公司。为什么？世界上有那么多事可以做，为什么要创办新公司？太难了。” （01:25:02）：我特别热爱能接触新体验的机会。我对物质并不执着，不想要名牌手表、豪车之类的东西，我只想看看世界。于是我想：“我要去伦敦生活三个月，再回旧金山待一个月，然后去墨西哥城生活三个月，尽情吸收各种体验。” 但这样做了六个月后，我意识到比起体验，我更在乎人际关系。如果你总是在飞机上追寻新体验，就很难建立和维系亲密、令人满足的关系。（01:25:47）：所以我回到旧金山，意识到如果想和朋友、志同道合的人保持联系，就不能满世界跑。周一早上，人们做什么？他们去上班。所以如果你想与他人互动，就要在他们周一早上待着的地方——工作场合——与他们交流。比起渴望创造产品（我确实有这个渴望），我更渴望合作，与他人共事。这就是我选择Snapchat的原因，也是我从追逐体验中抽身、重新投入建设的契机。正如我们已经描述的，后来我意识到：“我确实在乎这种合作，但或许不需要在世界上创造软件。” 而Quibi给了我机会，让我重新爱上这个过程。如今我们又回到了软件领域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Plus being on a board of a hardware company. What you just shared reminds me of Mark Manson's book, The Subtle Art of Not Giving a Fuck. Have you read this book?
turns.zh: 另外，我还在一家硬件公司的董事会任职。你刚才分享的内容让我想起了马克·曼森的《不给狗屁的微妙艺术》这本书。你读过这本书吗？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: I have not.
turns.zh: 我没读过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. It sold a bazillion copies, and the core of it is that we get joy out of solving problems and we think we'll be happy when we have freedom to do nothing. But it turns out freedom is only helpful to help us discover the problems we just want to keep solving.
turns.zh: 好的。这本书销量巨高，核心观点是我们从解决问题中获得快乐，认为只要获得了自由就可以什么都不做。但事实证明，自由只会帮助我们发现那些我们想继续解决的问题。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: Yeah, totally. I think that's exactly right. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，完全同意。我觉得你说得很对。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It sounds like that's the experience you went on. Last question, this new segment, I'm going to call Contrarian Corner. And the question is, is there something that you have a contrarian opinion about, something that you believe that most other people don't?
turns.zh: 听起来你就有过这样的经历。最后一个问题，这个新环节我称之为"反叛者角落"。问题是，你有没有什么相反的观点？就是大多数人不认同的观点？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: There's a segment in our industry that believes this very intensely, which is there's this belief that everybody needs to be a founder. And I think in some ways our industry would be much better off if there were fewer founders. I use an entire category of smart, creative, hardworking, talented, borderline visionary people who can raise that $2 million seed and go off and build some stupid company that's never going to go anywhere, that would be so much better off finding a team that needs their skillset and working on a problem that has, as I described, the mathematical formula that's going to win, that has the market opportunity that's the right size, that has the 10X thinking that can really... And I'm a little biased here because while I am a CEO for the first time now, I've never been a founder and I've been lucky enough to find a bunch of young teams that could benefit from my skills and enthusiasms, and sometimes to some success and sometimes to some embarrassment, but always really, really interesting. (01:28:53): Yeah. If you're out there and you think that the only possible way you can be successful in this industry on any metric, whatever metric you care about: you want the acclaim of your peers, you want financial reward, you want any of the things that people aspire to, outside impact on culture, whatever the thing is that gets you out of bed every morning, you can achieve that in collaboration with others. You don't have to be the person that raises the seed round.
turns.zh: 我们行业里有一些人对此深信不疑，他们认为每个人都必须成为创始人。我认为，如果创始人少一些，我们这个行业会好得多。我指的是那些认为每个人都必须成为创始人的人。我见过很多聪明、有创造力、勤奋、有才华、近乎有远见的人，他们能筹到200万美元种子资金，然后去创办一些永远不会成功的愚蠢公司。如果这些人能加入一个需要他们技能和热情的团队，解决一个有数学公式能获胜、有合适规模的市场机会、能激发10倍思维的难题，那他们会更有价值。（01:28:53）：是啊。如果你身处这个行业，认为在任何衡量标准上成功的唯一途径——无论你关心的标准是什么：你想获得同行的认可，获得经济回报，获得人们渴望的任何东西，对文化产生外部影响，或者是每天激励你起床的动力——你都可以通过与他人合作来实现这些目标。你不必成为筹集种子轮资金的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I 100% agree with that. I'm always telling people, "Don't start a company. It's super painful, very rarely works out. It's so hard." I don't know what's harder, being a product manager or being a founder, probably being a founder. They're both very hard.
turns.zh: 我完全同意这一点。我总是告诉人们：“别创办公司。这太痛苦了，很少成功。太难了。” 我不知道哪个更难，是产品经理还是创始人，可能还是创始人更难。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: Yeah, it is quite hard too. Yeah. Yeah. And just to be perfectly clear, there's something really special about founders. At both Pandora and now at Zero, the actual founders have from time to time said, "Well, you're like a founder." And I'm like, "I'm nothing like a founder. You took all the risk. When I showed up, there was a team and there was momentum and there was money in the bank. I appreciate your desire to say complimentary things, but 'You're like a founder' is not one that I'll take."
turns.zh: 是啊，也确实很难。是的。是的。说真的，创始人确实有一些特别之处。在Pandora和现在的Zero，真正的创始人有时会说：“嗯，你就像个创始人。” 我会说：“我一点都不像创始人。风险都是你们承担的。我出现的时候已经有团队、有势头、有银行存款了。我很感激你们想说些赞美的话，但‘你像个创始人’这种话我可不接受。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好了，我们进入令人兴奋的闪电问答环节了。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: I am ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 有什么书是你最常向别人推荐的？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: I really love Elad Gil's High Growth Handbook. It's organized into chapters about foundational company building, building a leadership team, building a board, and in addition to the thoughtful synthesis on that topic from Elad, he has an interview of someone that he does relevant to that section on each of the chapters. Really, really great read and super actionable if you're a leader in a young company. In a completely different end of the spectrum, I love big, complicated science fiction and there's a lot of garbage science fiction out there to be sure, but when you find something special, it's the best. So probably through the years in that category, there's a book called Hyperion by Dan Simmons. That's just a total classic. Everybody should read it.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢埃拉德·吉尔的《高增长手册》。这本书分章节讲解了公司的基础建设、领导团队的组建、董事会的搭建等内容。除了埃拉德对这些主题的深入总结外，每个章节还附有与该章节相关人物的访谈。对于初创公司的领导者来说，这本书真的非常实用且具有指导意义。说到完全不同的领域，我喜欢宏大复杂的科幻小说。虽然市面上有很多粗制滥造的科幻作品，但当你发现特别出色的作品时，那真是无与伦比的体验。比如丹·西蒙斯的《超新星》系列，堪称经典之作，每个人都应该读一读。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I read that. I think I read the first couple in the first one.
turns.zh: 我读过。我记得读过第一部的开头几章。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: Yeah. There is a sequel that's exceptional as well. And it's probably worth warning your readers that Hyperion is quite long and has an absolute cliffhanger.
turns.zh: 是啊，后续的续集也非常精彩。不过要提醒读者，《超新星》篇幅很长，悬念迭起。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think they're making a show out of it, which is going to be wild. I don't know how they do a show around that book. I thought you were going to say this other book, A Fire Upon the Deep. Have you heard of this book?
turns.zh: 我觉得他们要把它拍成剧集，这应该会很精彩。我不知道他们怎么能把这本书改编成电视剧。我还以为你说的是另一本《深渊上的火》呢。你听说过这本书吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think I only read the first one. Also, Three-Body Problem is the other one that I always think about. It's come up a couple of times on this podcast. Let's move on to the next question. Do you have a favorite recent movie or a TV show?
turns.zh: 对，我好像只读过第一本。另外，我一直想推荐的还有《三体》。这本书在播客里被提过好几次了。我们来回答下一个问题吧。你最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: I consume a lot of video content, both stuff that I'm very proud to talk about and stuff that I'm less proud to talk about, but I really liked the new Damon Lindelof show that's on Peacock called Mrs. Davis. So Lindelof, of course, from Lost and the new Watchmen on HBO, and Mrs. Davis is about an AI that you wear in your ear, like the HER AI and a nun that is hell-bent on the AI's destruction, and it reads like an early Coen brothers movie. It's super darkly funny and really, really thoughtful and unlike too much streaming, I think it's seven episodes, and it is a perfectly encapsulated story that has a beginning, middle, and an end and doesn't need to ever have another episode. It's amazing. Get yourself a Peacock subscription for at least a month to watch Mrs. Davis.
turns.zh: 我看了很多视频内容，有些值得骄傲地推荐，有些则不然。不过我真的很喜欢达蒙·林德洛夫在Peacock平台上的新剧《戴维斯夫人》。林德洛夫当然因《迷失》和HBO新版《守望者》而闻名，而《戴维斯夫人》讲的是一个植入耳朵的人工智能（类似HER AI）和一个决心摧毁人工智能的修女的故事，读起来像科恩兄弟早期的电影。它极其黑暗幽默，极具深度，与大多数流媒体作品不同，这部剧共七集，故事结构完整，有始有终，无需再拍续集。太棒了。大家可以去Peacock平台订阅至少一个月的会员观看《戴维斯夫人》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Favorite interview question you like to ask candidates that you're interviewing?
turns.zh: 你最喜欢问面试候选人的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: There are two things about interviews. The first is I always encourage people when they're thinking about their interview questions to take any question that they're tempted to pull from their own current experience with the goal of trying to, how would this person solve this thing that I'm working through right now? Because just causing the other person to speculate and oftentimes about your own business, I think you know really well that they don't actually know anything about, it creates this imbalance between the interviewer and the interviewee that feels out of sync with how I think about the collaborative nature of a great interview. So I tell people that almost every interview question should start with, "Tell me about a time in your career when..." to give them permission or to set their expectation that I'm asking them to tell me about something they've actually done that is relevant to the topic that I'm probing. (01:33:59): So that's just a structural thing that I try to do. And then usually towards the end of the interview, I ask almost everybody, "Imagine that you had a really great day at work. What was it that you did on that day?" Because what I'm trying to figure out is left to their own devices, what do they go to naturally because it rewards them? Because I think it's really important to find the highest best use of everyone you hire. And sometimes you can get a little bit to the bottom of what's the highest best use if you understand the things where there's a natural reward mechanism because it's like, "Well, I had this great day. I'm going to do more of that tomorrow." "What was the thing?" And it's just pretty illuminating.
turns.zh: 关于面试有两点需要注意。首先，我总是鼓励求职者在思考面试问题时，尽量从自己当前的经验中提取问题，比如：“请讲讲你职业生涯中某个与我现在面临的挑战类似的案例。” 这样做的好处是，既能让对方思考解决方案，又能避免让他们猜测你的业务细节。毕竟，求职者对你的业务并不熟悉，这种不对等的交流方式与我所推崇的合作式面试理念相违背。因此，我建议几乎所有面试问题的开头都用“请讲讲你职业生涯中某个……的经历”，让对方明白我希望他们分享与当前话题相关的真实经历。（01:33:59）这只是我努力遵循的结构规范。通常在面试尾声，我会问每个人：“想象你今天工作特别顺心，做了什么事呢？” 这样做能让我深入了解他们自然而然会去做的行为，因为这种行为能带来回报感。“嗯，我今天工作得很棒，明天还要继续保持这种状态。” 这种坦诚的反馈非常有启发性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 你最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: I have bought every pair of headphones on the planet, in part because Apple's headphones do not stay in my ears. I've sneezed one across the room, I've lost one down a drainpipe. They don't stay, none of them, the wired ones, the not wired ones, the in-ear ones, and it's left me feeling honestly like I am some kind of anatomical freak. I look at other people wearing them, I'm like, "What is going on with their ear that it's just staying there perfect?" It seems inconceivable to me. Nonetheless, I have a pair of AirPods Pro's that I want to love and put up with the fact that I'm going to drop them, lose them, sneeze them across the room. (01:35:32): But recently I came across this product from a company called Eartune that they're replacement tips and they just have the littlest bit of compression foam on them. They don't make the AirPods so big that they won't fit in the recharging case or anything, and they work. Miraculously, they stay in my ear. And Apple has this feature called Size Fit or something, go in settings, find your AirPods, scroll all the way down in the settings, and you can run this test where they play some audio and they tell you how good the seal is. And that revealed that my right ear is weirder than my left ear. So I actually have to use different tips in either sizes. Suddenly this sounds like a vaguely disgusting conversation that we're having. Anyway, I'm just really thrilled about my ability to wear Apple's AirPods after all these years.
turns.zh: 我买过市面上所有耳机，主要原因是苹果耳机总戴不稳。一次我打喷嚏把耳机扔到房间另一头，还有次掉进下水道了。无论有线耳机、无线耳机、入耳式耳机，都戴不稳，这让我怀疑自己是不是耳朵构造有问题。看着别人戴着耳机稳稳不掉，我总疑惑：“他们的耳朵怎么能完美贴合耳朵呢？” 这简直不可思议。不过我还是买了AirPods Pro，尽管容易掉、容易丢、容易被喷到房间另一头，但我还是想继续用它们。（01:35:32）最近我发现一家叫Eartune的公司推出的替换耳塞，表面覆盖了一层极薄的压缩泡沫。它们不会让AirPods变得过大而无法放进充电盒，同时效果惊人，耳塞能稳稳戴住。我还发现苹果有个“Size Fit”功能，在设置里找到AirPods，往下翻就能测试密封效果，结果显示我右耳比左耳更难适配，所以我得用不同尺寸的耳塞。这听起来像个有点尴尬的对话，但总之能在多年后成功佩戴AirPods让我特别兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think what we're learning is you are a mutant, your ears are different. Cool. We'll link to that product in the show notes.
turns.zh: 看来我们发现的是你是个异类，耳朵构造不同。不错。我们会在节目笔记里附上这款产品的链接。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to or share with friends, either in work or in life that you find useful?
turns.zh: 你有没有一个自己常回味或与朋友分享的生活格言，无论是在工作中还是生活中，觉得很有用的？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: You can't be a product person without having an eye rolly Charles Eames quote that's at the center of your existence. And for me, the Charles Eames quote is, "The details are not the details. They make the design." And I just really absolutely believe that, that the devil is in the details when you're a product designer and be uninterested in nuance at your peril.
turns.zh: 如果你不是产品经理，就不可能对查尔斯·伊姆斯（Charles Eames）的一句话深有共鸣，这句话构成了你存在的核心。对我来说，查尔斯·伊姆斯的名言是：“细节不是细节。它们成就了设计。” 我深信，当你是一名产品设计师时，魔鬼就藏在细节里，如果对微妙之处不感兴趣，那就是自找麻烦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. You worked with the creator of the GIF format. How does he pronounce, giff or jiff?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。你曾与GIF格式（Graphics Interchange Format）的发明者共事过。他怎么发音的？是jiff还是giff？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: Yeah. So before all of this, I worked at a company called CompuServe when I was in high school.
turns.zh: 是的。在高中时，我曾在一家叫CompuServe的公司工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: CompuServe, I used CompuServe. I didn't know that. That's amazing.
turns.zh: CompuServe，我用过CompuServe。我之前不知道。太惊人了。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: There was a guy on the team named Steve Wilhite who invented Graphics Interchange Format, GIF, and he was a straight out of central casting, 1960s neck beard programmer type, and the first I had ever encountered and very prickly. And it's crazy, but at the time, Steve would take all comers in the fight that it was pronounced jiff. Now he's obviously wrong. It's obviously pronounced giff. It's crazy to me now 35 years later, this is still a topic that pops up on the internet every once in a while. It's somehow like Zelig, I cross paths with the guy who created Graphics Interchange Format and I know his opinion on the topic even though it's an unpopular one.
turns.zh: 团队里有个叫史蒂夫·威尔海特（Steve Wilhite）的人，他发明了GIF格式。他就是那种典型的20世纪60年代的程序员，留着胡子，性格古怪。我当时还遇到过他，而且他脾气很坏。说来奇怪，当时史蒂夫坚持认为GIF应该发音为“jiff”。现在显然他错了。正确发音是“giff”。35年后的今天，这个话题偶尔还会在网上引发讨论。这就像《泽利格》（Zelig）一样，我偶然遇到了GIF格式的发明者，却还记得他对这个不受欢迎观点的看法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So he likes jiff, but you agree it's giff?
turns.zh: 明白了。所以他喜欢jiff，但你认为是giff？

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: It's definitely giff. It's obviously giff.
turns.zh: 肯定是giff。显然是giff。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. We're on the same page. We've decided. Let it be known.
turns.zh: 好的，太好了。我们达成共识了。就这么定了。让大家都知道。

turns.speaker: Tom Conrad
turns.en: Let it be known.
turns.zh: 让大家都知道。
